This means that because the self-nature and characteristics of intrinsic nature do not exist, all phenomena are unattainable; therefore, all phenomena are not subject to cessation.
Mahāmati, for what reason are all phenomena impermanent?
It refers to the impermanence of the arising of characteristics; therefore, it is said that all dharmas are impermanent.
Mahāmati, for what reason are all dharmas eternal?
"It means that because the nature of arising characteristics is non-arising, and because the impermanent is eternal, it is said that all phenomena are eternal.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"There are four kinds of categorical discourse: The direct response, the interrogative response,"
Through analysis and the cessation of discourse, one restrains all non-Buddhists.
Regarding existence and non-existence as arising, the teachers of Sāṃkhya and Vaiśeṣika declare that everything is indeterminate; such is what they demonstrate.
"What is discriminated by the Perfectly Awakened One has no self-nature that can be apprehended;
because it is free from verbal expression, it is said to be devoid of self-nature.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
We only pray that you will explain the general characteristics of the distinctions among the various types of *srotāpanna* and their respective destinies.

If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva thoroughly understands the general characteristics of the distinctions among the various types of *srotāpanna*, as well as the skillful means (*upāya*) of the *sakṛdāgāmin*, *anāgāmin*, and *arhat*, and having discerned them, may he preach the Dharma to sentient beings in such and such a manner.”

This refers to the characteristics of the two kinds of selflessness and the purification of the two obstacles; by transcending the characteristics of the various stages and attaining ultimate penetration, one realizes the inconceivable, ultimate realm of all Tathāgatas.
Like a mani jewel of manifold colors, it is well able to benefit all sentient beings, sustaining and nourishing them all with the inexhaustible body and wealth of the realm of all dharmas.
The Buddha told Mahāmati:
“Listen attentively, listen attentively!
Reflect upon it well.”
"I shall now explain it for you.
Mahāmati said to the Buddha,
"Excellent, World-Honored One!"
"So be it; we shall listen and receive [your teaching].
The Buddha told Mahāmati:
"There are three kinds of distinctions regarding the *srotāpanna* and the fruit of the *srotāpanna*."
What are the three?
They are the inferior, the middling, and the superior.
The inferior consists of at most seven more births;
The middling [type] attains parinirvāṇa after three or five births;
the superior [type] attains parinirvāṇa in that very birth.
These three types possess three fetters (saṃyojana), categorized as inferior, middling, and superior.
What are the three fetters?
They are the view of a self-identity, doubt, and attachment to precepts and rituals.
Through the progressive transcendence of these three fetters, one advances upward and attains arhatship.
Mahāmati! There are two kinds of the view of a self-body (satkāyadṛṣṭi):
namely, that which is innate and that which is conceptualized.
Just as there is the delusion of dependent origination and the delusion of intrinsic nature,
so too, based upon the dependent origination of intrinsic nature, various kinds of delusions regarding intrinsic nature arise through clinging.
Because that [nature] is neither existent, nor non-existent, nor both existent and non-existent, as it lacks the characteristics of real conceptualization;
yet foolish people, through their delusions, cling to various characteristics of the self-nature of conceptualization.
It is like a mirage in the heat, which causes thirsty deer to perceive it as water.

This is the false discrimination of the view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi) held by the Srotāpanna; through the realization of the non-self of persons (pudgalanairātmya), they grasp at the absence of intrinsic nature and thereby sever their long-standing ignorance and attachments.

Mahāmati! As for that which is co-nascent, it refers to the view of a self-body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) held by *srotāpannas*, because the four aggregates (*skandhas*)—both one's own body and those of others—are devoid of the characteristics of form (*rūpa*).

This is because form arises from the primary elements and their derivatives; because they are mutually dependent causes and conditions; and because the great elements and form do not aggregate [independently].
When a stream-enterer contemplates the view of the existence or non-existence of categories, the view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi) is severed.
When this view of a self is thus severed, craving does not arise; this is called the characteristic of the view of a self.
Mahāmati!

As for the characteristic of doubt: because one has attained the characteristic of correctly perceiving the Dharma, and because the two previous kinds of false conceptualization regarding the view of a self-body have been severed, doubt regarding the Dharma does not arise.
Not giving rise to the view of another as the Great Teacher regarding what is pure or impure—
this is called the characteristic of doubt that is severed by a Srotāpanna. Mahāmati!
Regarding the clinging to precepts (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*): why does the *srotāpanna* not cling to precepts?
It is because he clearly perceives the characteristics of suffering in the places where one is reborn; for this reason, he does not cling to them. Mahāmati!
"Grasping" refers to the fool's firm acceptance and practice of asceticism for the sake of various objects of pleasure, and thus seeking rebirth;

he does not grasp in this way, except for the dedication toward the excellence of self-awakening, being free from false conceptualization, and practicing the means of the characteristics of untainted dharmas while upholding the branches of the precepts—this is called the Stream-enterer’s severance of grasping at the characteristics of the precepts.
The stream-enterer has severed the three fetters, and craving and delusion do not arise.
If the stream-enterer were to think:
"These fetters are not realized by me," [he would fall into a misconception].
"There would be two faults: falling into the view of a self-body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), and the failure to sever the various fetters (*saṃyojana*).
Mahāmati said to the Buddha, "World-Honored One!"
“The World-Honored One has spoken of many forms of craving; which among them is the craving that is to be severed?
The Buddha told Mahāmati:

“To be infatuated with and attached to women, to be greedily clinging through various means, and to commit evil deeds of body and speech—receiving pleasure in the present while planting the seeds of future suffering—such [craving] shall not arise.”
Why is this? Because they have attained the bliss of the correct reception of samādhi.
Therefore, their abandonment is not the abandonment of craving for the pursuit of nirvāṇa.
Mahāmati! What are the characteristics of a Sakṛdāgāmin?
It is said that they suddenly perceive the characteristics of form and the characteristics of the arising of false discrimination, such that the characteristics of [subjective] vision do not arise.

Because he has clearly perceived the characteristics of the meditative attainments, he comes suddenly to this world to reach the end of suffering and attain nirvana; for this reason, he is called a Sakṛdāgāmin.
Mahāmati!
What is meant by an Anāgāmin?

It refers to one who perceives the faults inherent in the arising of past, future, and present forms—whether they possess characteristics or lack them—and because they prevent deluded thoughts from arising and have severed the fetters, they are called an Anāgāmin.
Mahāmati!

An Arhat is so called because the various dhyānas, samādhis, liberations, powers, and insights are, by nature, not subject to afflictions, suffering, or false conceptualization; therefore, they are named Arhats.
Mahāmati said to the Buddha:
"World-Honored One!
The World-Honored One has spoken of three kinds of arhats; which of these arhats is being referred to here?"
"Bhagavān!
Have you attained the path of the single vehicle of tranquility?
Or is it that you have manifested as an arhat through the skillful means of a bodhisattva mahāsattva?"
"Are they Śrāvakas transformed by the Buddha's emanations?
The Buddha told Mahāmati:
"They are Śrāvakas who have attained the path of the single vehicle of tranquility, and none other."

As for the others, they practice the bodhisattva path and manifest births within great assemblies through the power of their skillful means and original vows, as well as through the Buddha’s transformative emanations, in order to adorn the Buddha’s retinue.
Mahāmati! Within the realm of conceptual construction, various teachings are expounded concerning the attainment of fruits and the attainment of dhyāna.

Because those who enter dhyāna have completely transcended [dualistic grasping], they manifest the attainment of the measure of what is manifested by their own minds; this manifestation of the signs of attainment is termed "attainment of fruit."
Furthermore, Mahāmati!
Those who wish to transcend the realms of dhyāna, the immeasurables, and the formless should abandon the marks of what is manifested by their own minds. Mahāmati!
To say that one transcends the manifestation of one’s own mind through the attainment of cessation of sensation and perception is not so.
Why? Because there is the measure of mind (cittamātra).
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
“The various dhyānas and the four immeasurables, The formless attainments and samādhis,
And the cessation of all sensation and perception— In those [realms], even the measure of mind does not exist.”
The fruit of srotāpanna, the sakṛdāgāmin, the anāgāmin, and the arhat—these are all delusions of mind.
For the meditator, both meditation and its objects are such; it is the knowledge of their cessation that is the true reality.
This is merely the measure of deluded thought; if one awakens to this, there is liberation.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are two kinds of awakening, namely:
There is the realization through investigation and the realization established by the grasping and attachment to the characteristics of conceptual construction.

Mahāmati, as for the realization through investigation: it refers to the realization that the self-nature and characteristics of phenomena cannot be apprehended when analyzed and separated from the four extremes; this is called the realization through investigation.
Mahāmati!
Those four positions refer to being free from identity and difference, bothness and neitherness, existence and non-existence, and permanence and impermanence; these are called the four positions.
Mahāmati!
This freedom from these four positions is called "all dharmas.
Mahāmati!
One should study and practice these four lines of inquiry for observing all phenomena.
Mahāmati, what is the awakening that establishes through the grasping and attachment to the characteristics of false conceptualization?
That is to say:

the grasping of the characteristics of false discrimination, the attachment to the unreal characteristics of the four great elements—solidity, moisture, heat, and motion—and the establishment based on the attachment to propositions, reasons, concepts, and analogies;
this establishment of what is unreal is called the awakening that consists in the grasping of the characteristics of false discrimination and the attachment to its establishment.
These are called the two characteristics of awakening.

If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva accomplishes these two characteristics of awakening, they will reach the ultimate realization of the selflessness of persons and phenomena, and will skillfully know the awakening to non-existence through expedient means.

Observing the stages of practice, one attains the first stage (*bhūmi*), enters a hundred samādhis, and acquires various samādhis; one beholds a hundred Buddhas and a hundred bodhisattvas, and knows the events of a hundred kalpas in both the past and future limits;
light illuminates a hundred lands, one knows the characteristics of the progressively higher stages, and possesses the sovereign power of great vows and sublime spiritual faculties.

Through the empowerment of the Cloud of Dharma, one shall attain the stage of the Tathāgata’s self-awakening; by skillfully binding the mind to the ten inexhaustible phrases, one brings sentient beings to maturity, manifests various transformations, and is adorned with radiance, thereby attaining the samādhi of the noble bliss of self-awakened realization.
"Furthermore, Mahāmati!
A bodhisattva-mahāsattva should be skilled in the four great elements and derived form (*bhautika-rūpa*).
How does a bodhisattva become skilled in the four great elements and derived form?"
Mahāmati! When Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas train in this manner, they regard that which is the ultimate truth as the non-arising of the four great elements.
Regarding that non-arising of the four great elements, they engage in such contemplation.

Having observed this, one realizes the limits of the conceptualization of names and marks, the limits of what is manifested by one's own mind, and that external natures lack inherent existence; this is called the limit of the conceptualization of what is manifested by one's own mind.

This means that one contemplates the three realms as being devoid of the nature of the four great elements and their derived matter; the four propositions are universally purified, and one is detached from self and what belongs to self.
Abiding within the limits of the true mark and its own characteristic, the unarisen own-characteristic is established.
Mahāmati! How do those four great elements give rise to derived matter (*bhautika*)?

It is said that the great element of the delusion of moisture gives rise to the internal and external water element; the great element of the delusion of capability gives rise to the internal and external fire element; the great element of the delusion of movement gives rise to the internal and external wind element; and the great element of the delusion of the fragmentation of form gives rise to the internal and external earth element.
When form and space coexist, one becomes attached to false truths; the five aggregates gather, and the derived matter of the four great elements arises.
Mahāmati! As for consciousness, because it takes pleasure in various traces and objective realms, it continues on into other destinies.

Mahāmati! The four great elements, such as earth, and the derived forms, have the four great elements as their conditions, yet they do not have those [very] four great elements as their conditions. Why is this?
That is to say, when the nature, form, characteristics, place, and the application of means are without intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), the great elements (*mahābhūta*) do not arise. Mahāmati!
It is through the conjunction of nature, form, characteristics, place, and the application of means that they arise; it is not that they arise without form.
Therefore, the characteristics of the derived matter of the four great elements are the false imaginings of non-Buddhists;
they are not mine. Furthermore, Mahāmati!
Now, the intrinsic characteristics of the aggregates shall be explained.
What are the intrinsic characteristics of the aggregates?
They are the five aggregates.
What are the five?
They are form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
Among them, the four aggregates that are non-material are feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
Mahāmati! As for form, it consists of the four great elements and the derivative forms, each having distinct characteristics. Mahāmati!
The formless realm is not characterized by the number four, just as space is not.
For example, space transcends numerical characteristics and is free from numbers, yet through false conceptualization, one speaks of "one space."
Mahāmati!
Thus, these aggregates (skandhas) transcend the characteristics of number and are free from number; they are free from existence and non-existence, and free from the four propositions (catuṣkoṭi).
These characteristics of number are the discourse of the ignorant; what is spoken therein does not belong to the noble ones (ārya).
Mahāmati!
The various forms and images of the noble ones are like illusions, free from the conceptualization of difference or non-difference.
They are also like dreams, reflections, or the body of a person, because they are free from difference or non-difference.
Mahāmati! The realm of noble wisdom appears as the same as the false discrimination of the aggregates;
this is called the characteristic of the self-nature of the aggregates.
You should eliminate them; having eliminated them, you shall preach the Dharma of tranquility, severing all non-Buddhist views in all Buddha-fields.
Mahāmati! When preaching tranquility, the view of the selflessness of phenomena (dharmanairātmya) is purified, and one enters the Immovable Stage (acalā-bhūmi).

Having entered the Immovable Stage (*acalā-bhūmi*), they attain mastery over immeasurable samādhis and obtain the mind-made body (*manomaya-kāya*). Having attained the illusion-like samādhi (*māyopama-samādhi*) and reached ultimate penetration, they exercise sovereign power through their strengths and insights to rescue, sustain, and benefit all sentient beings.
"Just as the great earth supports and nurtures all living beings,
so too does the bodhisattva-mahāsattva universally rescue all beings.
Furthermore, Mahāmati!"
The various non-Buddhist outsiders have four kinds of nirvana.
What are the four? They are as follows:

Nirvana as the non-existence of the intrinsic nature of self-nature; nirvana as the non-existence of the various characteristics of self-nature; nirvana as the awakening to the non-existence of the self-characteristics of self-nature; and nirvana as the severance of the continuous flow of the individual and common characteristics of the aggregates.
These are called the four kinds of nirvāṇa of the various non-Buddhists;
they are not the Dharma taught by me, Mahāmati!
"What I have taught is that the cessation of the conceptualizing consciousness is called nirvana.
Mahāmati said to the Buddha,
"World-Honored One!"
"Do you not establish the eight consciousnesses? The Buddha said, "I do."
Mahāmati said to the Buddha:
"If there is an establishment [of consciousness], why is it that one is freed from the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) and not the seven consciousnesses?
The Buddha told Mahāmati:
"Because of those causes and those objects of perception, the seven consciousnesses do not arise.

As for the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), it arises through the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) produced by attachment to the segmentation of its objects; it nourishes the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) and functions in conjunction with the *manas*."
The conceptualization of "I" and "mine" arises from causes and conditions.

Not destroying the body-characteristics of the *ālayavijñāna*, it arises through clinging to objects manifested by one's own mind; thus, the collection of mental states arises, mutually dependent upon one another.
It is like the waves of the ocean: when stirred by the wind of objects manifested from one's own mind, they arise and cease in the same manner.
Therefore, when the *manovijñāna* (consciousness) ceases, the seven consciousnesses also cease.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
“I have no nature of nirvāṇa; It is the activity, the characteristics, And the consciousness of parikalpita and paratantra— When these cease, I am in nirvāṇa.”
With that as cause and that as object-condition, the mental tendencies (saṃskāra) and so forth form the body;
the mind is the giver of the cause, serving as the support for consciousness.
Just as when the great flow of water is exhausted, the waves do not arise.
In this way, when the mental consciousness ceases, the various forms of consciousness do not arise.
Furthermore, Mahāmati,
I shall now explain the general characteristics of the discrimination of the self-nature of conceptual construction (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).

If you and the other bodhisattva-mahāsattvas thoroughly discern the common characteristics through the discrimination of the nature of false imagination, you will leave behind false imagination and reach the noble realization of self-awareness. You will skillfully perceive the common goal of the non-Buddhists, and by awakening, you will sever the false imagination of the grasped and the grasper.
The various characteristics of dependent origination are the activities of the imagined nature; one no longer engages in such imagination.
Mahāmati, what is the common characteristic of the discrimination of the imagined nature?
That is to say:

the conceptualization of verbal expression, the conceptualization of the referent of what is expressed, the conceptualization of marks, the conceptualization of benefit, the conceptualization of self-nature, the conceptualization of cause, the conceptualization of views, the conceptualization of establishment, the conceptualization of arising, the conceptualization of non-arising, the conceptualization of continuity, and the conceptualization of bondage and non-bondage.
This is called the general characteristic of the discrimination of the nature of false imagination.
Mahāmati, what is the discrimination of verbal expression?
That is to say:
the sounds of various wonderful melodies and songs, and the attachment to such pleasant music—this is called the conceptualization of verbal expression. Mahāmati!
What is the conceptualization of the object of discourse?
It refers to the intrinsic nature of the object of discourse, which is known by noble wisdom.
Based upon that, there arises discursive conceptualization of verbal expression;
this is called the conceptualization of the object to be expressed. Mahāmati!
What is the delusion of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-vikalpa*)?
It refers to the various attachments to those very things previously mentioned, clinging to them just as a deer clings to the appearance of water in a mirage.
That is to say:
the characteristics of solidity, moisture, warmth, and motion; these are the false imaginings regarding all natures.
This is called the false imagining of characteristics.
Mahāmati! What is the discrimination of benefit?
It is as follows:
To delight in various kinds of gold, silver, and precious jewels—
this is called false conceptualization, Mahāmati.
What is the delusion of intrinsic nature?
It refers to the apprehension that "intrinsic nature exists as such."
It is not different from the false discrimination of evil views;
this is called the false discrimination of intrinsic nature. Mahāmati!
What is the discrimination of causes?
It refers to the arising of the marks of causes through the conceptualization of existence and non-existence regarding either causes or conditions.
This is called the delusion of causes.
Mahāmati, what is the delusion of views?
That is to say:
there are evil views concerning existence and non-existence, identity and difference, bothness and not-bothness; these are the deluded imaginings and attachments of externalists.
This is called the delusion of views.
Mahāmati! How is conceptualization established?
It is as follows:
The notions of "self" and "what belongs to self" constitute a dogmatic theory;
this is called the establishment of delusive discrimination.
"Mahāmati! [This is what I mean]."
What is the conceptualization of arising?
It refers to the attachment that arises based on the nature of existence and non-existence.
This is called the delusion of arising. Mahāmati,
what is the delusion of non-arising?
That is to say:
all natures are fundamentally unarisen.
Without seeds or causal conditions, they give rise to a body that is itself causeless.
This is called the delusion of non-arising.
Mahāmati, what is the delusion of continuity?
That is to say:
their mutual continuity is like gold and thread;
this is called the delusion of continuity.
Mahāmati! What is the discrimination of bondage and non-bondage?
It is as follows:
Attachment to the causes and conditions of bondage—
such as the efforts of a person to either bind or liberate—
is called the false discrimination of bondage and non-bondage.
Regarding these common characteristics of the discrimination of the nature of false imagination, all foolish people cling to existence and non-existence.
Mahāmati, those who cling while clinging to dependent origination are clinging to the nature of various false imaginations.
Just as an illusion manifests various bodies, ordinary people, through their false imaginings, perceive various different illusions.
Mahāmati! Illusion and the various [forms] are neither different nor not different.
If they were different, the illusion would not be the cause of the various manifestations;
if they were not different, there would be no distinction between the illusion and the various manifestations, yet a distinction is perceived.
Therefore, they are neither different nor non-different.
Therefore, Mahāmati!

You and the other Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should not cling to the notion that the nature of false discrimination arising from conditions—which is like an illusion—is either different or not different, existent or non-existent.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"The mind is bound by objects; Discriminative thought and cognition follow along with them.
When there is nothing [to grasp] and the supreme [realization], The wisdom of equality arises."
The self-nature of false imagination exists, yet it does not exist within dependent origination;
false imagination may be grasped, but dependent origination is not false imagination.
When various constituent parts arise, they do not truly exist, being like a magical illusion.
Those signs are manifold, yet through false conceptualization they are not established.
Those signs are indeed errors, all arising from the bondage of the mind;
false conceptualization has no object of knowledge, for it is a conceptualization regarding dependent origination.
The nature of these various conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) is itself dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*);
though conceptual constructions are manifold, they arise from dependent origination. There are three [types of arising]:
the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), and the third, which arises without cause.
Conceptual construction explains the conventional truth; its cessation is the realm of the sages.
Just as in the practice of cultivation, a single thing appears as manifold, yet within it there is no multiplicity—such is the nature of conceptual construction.
Just as various cataracts cause manifold forms to appear through false conceptualization,
yet the cataract itself is neither form nor non-form, so it is with the failure to realize dependent origination.
Just as refined pure gold is free from all impurities, [so too is the nature of reality].
As space is free from clouds and obscurations, so too is the purity of false conceptualization (vikalpa).
There is no intrinsic nature of false conceptualization, nor is there that which arises through conditions;
both establishment and denial are entirely destroyed by false conceptualization.
If false imagination has no intrinsic nature, yet there is the nature of dependent origination,
then from the absence of nature there arises nature, and from nature there arises the absence of nature.
Depending upon false imagination as its cause, one attains that dependent origination.
Names and characteristics always follow one another, giving rise to all manner of false imaginings.
When these are ultimately not established, one transcends all such imaginings;
only then does one know purity—this is called the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
There are twelve kinds of conceptual construction, and six kinds of dependent origination;
when one personally realizes suchness, there is no distinction between them.
The five dharmas constitute reality, and self-nature is of three kinds.
Practicing the discernment of this does not transcend suchness (*tathatā*).
The various marks and dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) are called the arising of false conceptualization (*vikalpa*);
those various marks of false conceptualization arise from that dependent origination.
When awakened wisdom observes well, there is no objective condition and no conceptual construction;
once established, it has no inherent nature. How, then, could there be an awakening to conceptual construction?
From that nature of conceptual construction, the two natures are established.
Diverse manifestations appear through false conceptualization; they are the pure realm of the sages.
False conceptualization is like the colors in a painting; it is based on dependent origination yet reckoned as false conceptualization.
If it were different from false conceptualization, it would simply be the doctrine of the non-Buddhists.
"What is conceptualized is spoken of through false imagination; it arises from the conjunction of views.
One who is free from these two types of false imagination—in this way, they achieve success.
Mahāmati Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

We only pray that you will explain the characteristics of the noble wisdom of self-realization and the One Vehicle. If you explain the characteristics of the noble wisdom of self-realization and the One Vehicle, I and the other bodhisattvas will thoroughly realize the characteristics of the noble wisdom of self-realization and the One Vehicle for ourselves, without depending on others, and thereby penetrate the Buddha-dharma.”
The Buddha told Mahāmati:
“Listen attentively, listen attentively!
Reflect upon it well, and I shall explain it for you.”
Mahāmati said to the Buddha,
“Yes, I shall receive your instruction.
The Buddha told Mahāmati:

"What was known by the former sages has been transmitted from one to another; yet, conceptualization (vikalpa) is devoid of intrinsic nature. When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas dwell alone in a quiet place, they observe through self-awakening without depending on others. Having abandoned the conceptualizations of views, they advance higher and higher until they enter the stage of the Tathāgata; this is called the characteristic of the noble wisdom of self-awakening."
Mahāmati! What are the characteristics of the One Vehicle?
They are as follows:
I speak of the One Vehicle because one attains awakening to the path of the One Vehicle.
What is meant by attaining awakening to the path of the One Vehicle? It is as follows:
When the false discrimination of the grasped and the grasper does not arise in its true state, this is called the awakening of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*).

Mahāmati, this awakening of the One Vehicle cannot be attained by others—neither by outsiders, nor by Śrāvakas, nor by Pratyekabuddhas, nor by Brahmā-devas and the like; it can be attained only by the Tathāgata.
"For this reason, it is called the One Vehicle.
Mahāmati said to the Buddha,
"World-Honored One, for what reason do you speak of three vehicles rather than one vehicle?"
The Buddha told Mahāmati:
"Because they do not possess the nature of attaining parinirvāṇa by themselves, I do not teach that all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas share a single vehicle (ekayāna).

All śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas attain liberation through the Tathāgata’s subduing and the bestowal of skillful means for tranquility, rather than by their own power; therefore, I do not speak of a single vehicle."
"Furthermore, Mahāmati!
Because the habitual tendencies of the afflictive obscurations and karma have not been severed, I do not speak of a single vehicle (ekayāna) for all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
Because they do not realize the selflessness of phenomena (dharmanairātmya) and have not transcended death within the realm of分段死 (paricchedamaraṇa), I speak of three vehicles."

Mahāmati! Those who have severed all the habitual tendencies of the faults arising from afflictions, as well as those who have realized the selflessness of phenomena—they have severed all the habitual tendencies of the faults arising from afflictions;
they do not cling to the flavor of the bliss of samādhi, and they realize the untainted realm (anāsrava-dhātu).
Having awakened, he further enters the supramundane, most excellent, and untainted realm; fulfilling all requisites, he shall attain the Tathāgata’s inconceivable and sovereign Dharma-body.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
“The vehicle of the devas and the Brahmās, the vehicle of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas,
and the vehicle of the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas— these various vehicles I have taught.”
As long as the mind continues to function, the various vehicles are not ultimate.
When that mind is extinguished, there is neither vehicle nor one who rides it;
since no establishment of vehicles exists, I teach what is called the One Vehicle.
In order to guide sentient beings, I distinguish and teach the various vehicles.
There are three kinds of liberation, as well as the selflessness of phenomena;
regarding afflictions and wisdom, etc., liberation is their complete transcendence.
Just as a piece of wood floating on the ocean Is constantly turned by the waves,
So too are the ignorant śrāvakas, Driven about by the winds of signs.
When their afflictions arise and then cease, They remain deluded regarding the habituation of those afflictions.
Relishing the bliss of samādhi, they dwell securely in the untainted realm (*anāsrava-dhātu*).
Having no ultimate destination, yet not retreating either,
they attain a body of various samādhis, remaining unawakened for as long as an eon.
Just as a person who is intoxicated awakens only after the wine has worn off, so too is the awakening to the Dharma;
one thereby attains the supreme body of a Buddha. *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, Fascicle II.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati, saying:
"I shall now explain the characteristics of the various types of the mind-made body (*manomaya-kāya*).
Listen attentively, listen attentively!"
"Reflect upon this well.
Mahāmati said to the Buddha,
"Excellent, World-Honored One!"
"So be it; we shall receive your instruction.
The Buddha told Mahāmati:
"There are three kinds of mind-made bodies (manomaya-kāya)."
What are these three? They are:

the mind-made body born of the meditative absorption in the bliss of samādhi; the mind-made body born of the realization of the self-nature of phenomena; and the mind-made body born of the spontaneous manifestation of its kind, which is free from effortful activity.
The practitioner, having fully understood the signs of progress on the first stage, attains three kinds of bodies.
Mahāmati, what is the mind-made body attained through the correct meditative absorption of the bliss of samādhi?
That is to say:

in the third, fourth, and fifth stages, because of the correct meditative attainment (*samādhi-sukha-samāpatti*), various [states of] one's own mind become tranquil; one dwells securely in the ocean of the mind, and the marks of the surging waves of consciousness do not arise. Knowing that the nature of the objects appearing from one's own mind is neither existent nor non-existent—this is called the "mind-made body born of the correct meditative attainment of bliss."
Mahāmati! What is the mind-made body resulting from the realization of the self-nature of dharmas?
It is as follows:

In the eighth stage, one observes and realizes that all phenomena, such as illusions and the like, are entirely non-existent. There occurs a transformation of body and mind, whereby one attains the illusion-like samādhi and other gateways of samādhi, as well as immeasurable marks, powers, masteries, and clarities. Adorned like exquisite flowers, moving with swiftness according to one's will—like an illusion, a dream, the moon in water, or a reflection in a mirror—it is neither created nor created from causes, yet it appears as if created and produced from causes. Fully endowed with all varieties of physical forms and limbs, it enters into all Buddha-fields and great assemblies. Because it penetrates the nature of selflessness in all phenomena, this is called the "mind-made body born of the realization of the self-nature of dharmas."
Mahāmati!
What is the body born of mind, which is innate to its kind and free from volitional effort?
It is as follows:
Awakening to all Buddha-dharmas and realizing the mark of joy attained through one's own realization— this is called the "body born of mental attention that is innate and of the same nature.
Mahāmati, you should study and cultivate the observation and thorough understanding of these three types of bodily marks.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"It is not that I ride the Great Vehicle; It is neither speech nor letters.
It is not the Truths, nor is it liberation; Yet it is not without a realm."
"However, by riding upon the Mahāyāna, one attains mastery over samādhi;
with various mind-made bodies, one is adorned with the flowers of sovereignty.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
As the World-Honored One has said, if a man or a woman commits the five deeds of immediate retribution, they do not enter the Avīci Hell.
World-Honored One!”
"How is it that men and women who commit the five deeds of immediate retribution do not enter the Avīci Hell?
The Buddha told Mahāmati:
"Listen attentively, listen attentively!"
"Reflect upon this well; I shall speak for your sake.
Mahāmati said to the Buddha, "Excellent, World-Honored One!"
"Indeed, we shall receive your instruction.
The Buddha told Mahāmati:
"What are the five deeds of immediate retribution?"
That is to say:
killing one's father and mother, harming an arhat, causing schism in the Saṃgha, and with an evil mind drawing blood from the body of a Buddha.
Mahāmati!
What is the mother of sentient beings?
It is craving that leads to renewed existence, accompanied by delight and lust.

Just as one is established by depending on a mother, with ignorance as the father, they give birth to the village of the sense bases (*āyatana*); to sever these two roots is called "killing one's parents.
When those underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) do not manifest—like the delayed onset of rat poison—to ultimately eradicate all phenomena and sever them is called "killing an Arhat."
What is meant by "breaking the Sangha"?
It refers to the ultimate severance of the accumulation and aggregation of the various aggregates (skandhas) which possess distinct characteristics; this is called breaking the Sangha.
Mahāmati!

Failing to realize that the external world—consisting of specific and general characteristics—is merely the manifestation of one's own mind, and failing to understand the sevenfold body of consciousness, one employs the three liberations and untainted perceptions of evil to ultimately sever those seven kinds of Buddha-consciousness; this is called shedding the blood of a Buddha with an evil mind.
If men or women commit these acts of immediate retribution, they are called the five deeds of immediate retribution, and are also termed immediate karmas.
"Furthermore, Mahāmati!
There exists an external uninterrupted [state]; I shall now expound it.
Having heard this meaning, you and the other bodhisattva-mahāsattvas will not fall into delusion in future ages.
What are the five immediate transgressions?
They are the immediate transgressions previously mentioned.
If one practices this, one will not attain the dharma of immediate realization (*ānantarya*) in each of the three liberations.
Apart from these dharmas, there are other transformed powers that manifest as immediate realization;

namely, the transformative power of Śrāvakas, the transformative power of Bodhisattvas, and the transformative power of Tathāgatas. For the sake of those who have committed the five heinous crimes (*ānantaryakāraka*), in order to eliminate their doubts and remorse and to inspire them, they employ transformative power to manifest such immediate realization.
There is no one who, by performing acts of immediate retribution, can fail to attain the dharmas of immediate realization,
provided they awaken to the fact that all is merely the manifestation of their own mind, abandon the delusions regarding body and wealth, and relinquish the grasping at "I" and "mine."
"Or at times, one may encounter a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) and be liberated from the delusive conceptualizations that cause the continuity of other realms of existence.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"Covetous craving is called the mother; Ignorance is the father."
Awakening to objects and consciousness as Buddha, The various proclivities as Arhats,
And the accumulation of the aggregates as the Saṅgha— To sever these in immediate succession Is called the five acts of immediate retribution; Yet one does not enter the Avīci Hell.
At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One,
I only pray that you will explain for me the Buddha’s knowledge and awakening."
“World-Honored One!
What is the Buddha’s knowledge and awakening?
The Buddha told Mahāmati:

"To realize the selflessness of persons and phenomena, to fully understand the two obstacles, to be free from the two kinds of death, and to sever the two afflictions—this is called the awakening of a Buddha.
If Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas attain this Dharma, they too are called Buddhas."
"For this reason, I teach the One Vehicle.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"Thoroughly knowing the two kinds of selflessness, The two obstacles and the afflictions are severed."
"Forever free from the two kinds of death—this is called the Buddha’s awakening.
At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
For what reason did the World-Honored One proclaim these words among the great assembly:

"I am all the Buddhas of the past," and further describe his various births, saying in the Sūtras of the Hundred Thousand Births: "At that time, I was the Cakravartin King Mandhātṛ, the six-tusked great elephant, the parrot bird, Śakra Devānām Indra, the Rishi Sunetra," and so forth?
The Buddha told Mahāmati:
“Because of the fourfold equality, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, proclaims these words among the great assembly:
‘At that time, I was Krakucchanda, Kanakamuni, and Kāśyapa Buddha.’”
"What are the four equalities? They are:
equality of letters, equality of speech, equality of dharmas, and equality of body; these are called the four equalities."
Because of four kinds of equality, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, proclaims these words in the great assembly.
What is the equality of syllables?
If the word designates me as a Buddha, that same word also designates all Buddhas; since the intrinsic nature of that word has no distinction, these names are equal.
What is meant by "equality of speech"? It is this:

my sixty-four kinds of vocal qualities arising from the Brahma-sound are produced; those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas likewise produce sixty-four kinds of vocal qualities arising from the Brahma-sound, without increase or decrease, without distinction, possessing the nature of the Brahma-sound of the kalaviṅka bird.
What is meant by "equality of body" (*kāya-samatā*)?

It means that there is no difference between myself and the Dharma-bodies and Form-bodies with their marks and signs of all Buddhas; except for the manifestation of various distinct Form-bodies in order to discipline sentient beings of various different destinies, this is called equality of body.
What is the equality of dharmas?
It means that I and those Buddhas have attained the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment.
Briefly stated, the unimpeded wisdom of the Buddha-dharma is called the four immeasurables.
For this reason, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, proclaims these words amidst the great assembly.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
“Kāśyapa, Krakucchanda, Kanakamuni, and I—
Because these four are equal, I have explained them for my sons.”
Mahāmati addressed the Buddha again, saying:
“As the World-Honored One has said:

‘From the night I attained supreme perfect enlightenment until the night I enter parinirvāṇa, not even a single word was spoken by me in the interval; nor was anything spoken, nor will anything be spoken. That which is not spoken is what is called the teaching of the Buddha.’”
Mahāmati said to the Buddha:
"World-Honored One!
For what reason did the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha say: "The Tathāgatas do not arise nor do they perish"? Why did he speak thus?"
"Why do you say, 'This is not spoken by the Buddha'?
The Buddha told Mahāmati:
"It is because of two factors that I have made such a statement."
What are the two dharmas? They are:
the dharma realized through one's own attainment and the dharma that has existed from the beginning; these are called the two dharmas.
It is because of these two dharmas that I speak thus.
What is the dharma realized through one's own attainment?
Whatever has been attained by those Tathāgatas, I too have attained; it is neither increased nor diminished.
Based on the ultimate realm of the Dharma realized by oneself, one is free from verbal conceptualization and free from the two paths of letters.
What is the primordially abiding Dharma?
It is as follows:

The ancient and primordial path of the sages is like the nature of gold, silver, and so forth; it is eternally abiding within the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu). Whether a Tathāgata appears in the world or does not appear, the dharma-realm remains eternally abiding.

Just as one proceeds toward the attainment of the Way—for example, like a man traveling through a vast wilderness who sees a level, direct road leading to an ancient city, and immediately follows it into the city to enjoy his heart’s desire—so it is here.
"Mahāmati!
What do you think? Did that man create this path and the various pleasures within the city?
He replied:
"No," [Mahāmati] replied.
The Buddha told Mahāmati:
"The dharma-realm of myself and all past Buddhas is eternally abiding; it is likewise so."
Therefore it is said:

"From the night I attained supreme perfect enlightenment until the night I enter parinirvāṇa, in the interval between these two times, I have not uttered a single word; nor have I spoken one, nor shall I speak one."
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"From the night I attained enlightenment until the night of my parinirvāṇa,
in the interval between these two, I have said nothing at all."
"Because I abide in the Dharma realized by myself, I have made this statement:
'That Buddha and I are entirely without distinction.
At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva again requested of the World-Honored One:

"I only pray that you will explain for me the characteristics of existence and non-existence regarding all phenomena, so that I and other bodhisattva-mahāsattvas may leave behind the characteristics of existence and non-existence and swiftly attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
The Buddha told Mahāmati:
"Listen attentively, listen attentively!
Reflect upon it well, and I shall explain it for you."
Mahāmati said to the Buddha:
“Excellent, World-Honored One!
We shall indeed receive your instruction.”
The Buddha told Mahāmati:
"This world has two kinds of dependence, namely:
dependence on existence and dependence on non-existence."
And falling into the views of existence and non-existence, they do not depart from the characteristic of departure. Mahāmati,
how does the world rely upon existence?
That is to say:
there is that which arises through worldly causes and conditions, and it is not non-existent.
From existence there is arising; it is not from non-existence that there is arising.
Mahāmati! Those who speak in such a manner are asserting that the world is without cause.
Mahāmati!
What is meant by the world depending on non-existence?

It refers to having first experienced the nature of greed, anger, and delusion, and subsequently engaging in false conceptualization and attachment regarding whether that nature of greed, anger, and delusion exists or does not exist.
Mahāmati! If one does not grasp at the existence of intrinsic nature, then the characteristics of that nature are quiescent.
Therefore, it is said that the Tathāgatas, Śrāvakas, and Pratyekabuddhas do not grasp at the nature of greed, hatred, and delusion as being either existent or non-existent.
“Mahāmati! Among these, what is it that destroys?
Mahāmati said to the Buddha:
“World-Honored One!
If one grasps the nature of greed, anger, and delusion, one will not grasp them again later.
The Buddha told Mahāmati:
“Excellent, excellent! It is well that you understand it thus,
Mahāmati!”
It is not only that the nature of greed, anger, and delusion, as well as their non-nature, are destroyed; it is also that Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and even Buddhas are destroyed. Why is this so?
This is because they cannot be apprehended internally or externally, and because the nature of the afflictions is neither different nor non-different [from them]. Mahāmati!

Greed, anger, and delusion—whether internal or external—cannot be apprehended; for the nature of greed, anger, and delusion is without body and without grasping. It is not the Buddhas, Śrāvakas, or Pratyekabuddhas who destroy them.
Because Buddhas, Śrāvakas, and Pratyekabuddhas are by nature liberated, bondage and the cause of bondage do not exist as intrinsic natures.
Mahāmati! If there were one who was bound, there would necessarily be bondage, because that [bondage] would be the cause of binding.
Mahāmati! Such a teaching of destruction is called the characteristic of non-existence. Mahāmati!
For this reason, I say that it would be better to hold a view of a personal self as large as Mount Sumeru than to give rise to the view of emptiness born of the overweening pride of "nothingness.
Mahāmati, those who possess the overweening pride of "nothingness" are said to be destroyers.
Falling into the views of self-characteristics and common characteristics, they long for them without knowing that these are merely the manifestations of their own minds.
They perceive external natures as impermanent, perishing moment by moment in succession;
they see the aggregates, elements, and sense bases as a continuous stream that undergoes transformation and cessation, yet they remain attached to the conceptualization of verbal signs.
"This is called a destroyer.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"Existence and non-existence are two extremes, Extending even to the realm of the mind."
Purifying those objects of perception, the mind of equanimity is stilled.
Without grasping at the nature of objects, cessation is not a state of nothingness;
all phenomena are thusness, like the sphere of the noble ones.
Arising without seeds, and ceasing once arisen;
existing through causes and conditions yet being non-existent—such a person does not abide in my teaching.
They are neither a non-Buddhist nor a Buddha; they are neither I nor anyone else.
Arising from the convergence of causes and conditions, how could it be non-existent?
Who asserts that what exists through the gathering of causes and conditions is instead non-existent?
Such proponents of false views generate theories regarding the arising of phenomena, falsely conceptualizing existence and non-existence through deluded imagination.
"If one knows that there is nothing produced, And likewise nothing extinguished,
Observing all this as entirely empty and quiescent, One is free from both existence and non-existence.
At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
We pray that you will explain for us and for all bodhisattvas the characteristics of the penetration of the ultimate principle (*siddhānta-yukti*).

If the characteristics of the penetration of the ultimate principle are skillfully distinguished, we and all bodhisattvas shall thoroughly understand these characteristics; having understood these characteristics, we shall swiftly attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and shall not follow after discursive perceptions, nor the various māras and externalists.”
The Buddha told Mahāmati:
"Listen attentively, listen attentively!
Reflect upon it well, and I shall explain it for you."
Mahāmati said to the Buddha,
“Yes, I shall receive your instruction.
The Buddha told Mahāmati:
“All śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas have two kinds of general characteristics, namely:
the penetration of the ultimate principle (zongtong) and the penetration of verbal teaching (shuotong). Mahāmati!..."
The "Principle of the Essential" (zongtong) refers to: the aspect of supreme advancement attained through one's own realization;

being far removed from the delusions of speech, words, and letters; proceeding toward the outflow-free realm (*anāsrava-dhātu*) and the specific characteristics of the stage of self-awakening; remaining far removed from all false perceptions and conceptualizations; subduing all external paths and hordes of Māras; and the radiance of the light of the path of self-awakening shining forth.
This is called the characteristic of the penetration of the ultimate truth (zongtongxiang).
What is the characteristic of the penetration of verbal teaching (shetongxiang)? It is as follows:

He expounds the various teachings of the nine divisions of scripture, which are free from characteristics such as difference and non-difference, existence and non-existence; employing skillful means, he teaches the Dharma in accordance with the capacities of sentient beings, enabling them to attain liberation.
This is called the characteristic of the communication of the teaching.
Mahāmati! You and the other bodhisattvas should practice and study this.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"The characteristics of the fundamental doctrine and the communication of teaching, The conditions of self-nature and the teachings of the Dharma—
If one perceives them well and distinguishes them clearly, One will not follow various conceptualizations."
There is no true reality, yet it is imagined by the foolish;
how can one give rise to the notion of desire?
Since non-nature is liberation, observe all conditioned phenomena as a continuous succession of arising and ceasing.
They increase two views and, being inverted, lack true knowledge.
One [view] is the ultimate truth; the absence of fault is nirvana.
Contemplating the world’s delusions, they are like illusions, dreams, and plantain trees.
"Though greed, hatred, and delusion exist, in reality there is no person;
from craving arise the aggregates, and all that exists is like a phantom or a dream.
At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
We pray that you will explain the characteristics of unreal conceptualization.
How does unreal conceptualization arise?”
"What kind of dharmas are called unreal conceptualization?
Within what kind of dharmas does unreal conceptualization occur?
The Buddha told Mahāmati:
“Excellent, excellent!
You are able to ask the Tathāgata about such a meaning; it will bring great benefit and great peace and happiness, out of compassion for all devas and humans in the world.”
"Listen attentively, listen attentively!
Reflect upon it well; I shall speak for your sake.
Mahāmati said to the Buddha:
“Excellent, World-Honored One!
We shall indeed receive your instruction.
The Buddha told Mahāmati:
“Mahāmati, various kinds of unreal conceptual attachments to diverse meanings give rise to discursive thought (*vikalpa*).

Mahāmati, by clinging to the grasped and the grasper, failing to understand that all is a manifestation of one's own mind, and falling into the views of existence and non-existence, one increases the views of the outsiders.”
"The habitual tendencies of false conceptualization lead to attachment to various external objects.
Through the false conceptualizations of the mind and mental factors, there arises attachment to 'self' and 'what belongs to self.
Mahāmati said to the Buddha:
“World-Honored One!
If various meanings and various unreal false imaginings arise from attachment to false imaginings;

if there is attachment to the grasped and the grasper; if one does not know that these are merely the manifestations of one’s own mind; and if one falls into the views of existence and non-existence, thereby increasing the views of the externalists.”
The habitual tendencies of false conceptualization lead to attachment to various external objects.
From these mental states and their associated mental factors, false conceptualizations arise, giving rise to attachment to "I" and "mine.
World-Honored One!
If such various external characteristics of objects fall into the marks of existence and non-existence, yet are free from being and non-being, and free from the marks of views—
World-Honored One,
the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) is likewise free from the marks of means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), limits, divisions, analogies, and causes.
"World-Honored One!

For what reason does false discrimination arise from attachment to the various natures of unreal meanings in a single location, rather than arising from attachment to the characteristics of the locus of the ultimate truth? Could it be that the World-Honored One is propounding a doctrine of false causes?"
"It speaks of one birth and one non-birth.
The Buddha told Mahāmati:
"It is not that false discrimination has one birth and one non-birth."
Why is this? It is because the false conceptualizations of existence and non-existence do not arise.

When one perceives that external objects are neither existent nor non-existent, and realizes them to be merely the manifestations of one’s own mind, false conceptualization (*vikalpa*) does not arise. Mahāmati,

I say that because of the various marks of false conceptualization within the minds of other ignorant people, their activities appear before them, and thus attachments to the nature and characteristics of those various conceptualizations arise.
How does a fool attain freedom from the views of clinging to "I" and "mine"?

By being free from the errors of cause, condition, agent, and action; by awakening to the mind-only nature of one's own delusive imaginings; by the transformation of body and mind; and by ultimately attaining clear understanding of all stages—the realm of the Tathāgata’s self-realization—thereby becoming free from the delusive imaginings regarding the five dharmas, the three natures, and the perception of things.
For this reason, I say that conceptual construction arises from attachment to various unreal objects.
By knowing the reality as it is, one attains liberation and brings to rest these various conceptual constructions.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"From various causes and conditions, the world arises;
Through false imaginings, one clings to the four extremes, Failing to know the penetration of my teaching."
The world is not born from existence, nor is it born from non-existence;
it is not born from both existence and non-existence, nor is it born from neither existence nor non-existence.
How can the ignorant harbor delusive thoughts regarding causes and conditions?
Neither existent nor non-existent, nor yet both existent and non-existent—thus one contemplates the world.
The mind is transformed and attains selflessness;
all natures are unarisen, because they arise from conditions.
All that is produced through conditions is not self-existent;
an entity does not produce itself, for there would be the fault of duality.
Since there is no fault of duality, no intrinsic nature can be found.
Observing all conditioned phenomena, which are free from the grasper and the grasped, and which are the measure of mind that is no-mind—I call this the measure of mind.
This measure is the locus of intrinsic nature; it is devoid of both the object and its cognitive nature.
The nature is ultimately wondrously pure; I declare this to be the measure.
The "self" established by conventional truth has no substantial reality;
the aggregates and the designation of "aggregates" are likewise without substance.
There are four kinds of equality: that of characteristics, that of the nature of causes, the third being the absence of self, and the fourth being the practitioner of cultivation.
Through the transformation of the habitual tendencies of false conceptualization, various kinds of minds arise.
Objects appear externally; this is the measure of the conventional mind.
Though appearing externally, they do not exist; the mind perceives their various forms.
Establishing [concepts of] body and property, I call this the measure of the mind.
Free from all views, and free from both the conceptualizer and the conceptualized;
without attainment and without arising—this I call the measure of mind (*cittamātra*).
Neither being nor non-being, it is entirely free from both being and non-being.
That which is called the liberation of the mind, I declare to be the measure of mind (cittamātra).
Suchness, the limit of emptiness, nirvāṇa, and the dharma-realm,
as well as the various types of mind-born bodies— I declare these to be the measure of mind.
At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
As the World-Honored One has taught, a bodhisattva-mahāsattva should be skilled in words and meanings."
What is meant by a bodhisattva’s skillful speech and meaning? What is speech?
What is meaning?
The Buddha told Mahāmati:
"Listen attentively, listen attentively!
Reflect upon it well, and I shall explain it for you."
Mahāmati said to the Buddha:
"Excellent, World-Honored One!
We shall indeed receive your instruction."
The Buddha told Mahāmati:
"What is speech? It is as follows:"

The conjunction of words and conceptualization arises based on the throat, lips, tongue, teeth, gums, and cheeks; it is produced through the attachment to the habitual tendencies of conceptualization resulting from those verbal expressions of "self" and "other."
This is called "language.
Mahāmati, what is meant by "meaning"?
That is to say:
being free from all characteristics of conceptual construction and characteristics of verbal expression— this is called "meaning," Mahāmati.

Regarding such meanings, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva, dwelling alone in a quiet place, through the wisdoms of hearing, reflection, and cultivation, takes as an object his own self-awakened realization and heads toward the city of nirvāṇa; having transformed the body of habitual tendencies, he realizes his own awakened realm and contemplates the signs of the progressive advancement between each stage.
This is called the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s skill in meaning.
Furthermore, Mahāmati,
the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva skilled in the meaning of speech contemplates that speech and its meaning are neither different nor not different.
The relationship between meaning and language is likewise so.
If language were different from meaning, one could not discern meaning through language; rather, one enters into meaning by means of language, just as a lamp illuminates forms.
Furthermore, Mahāmati!

Regarding non-arising and non-ceasing, intrinsic nirvāṇa, the three vehicles and the one vehicle, and the self-nature of the mind—when one becomes attached to the meanings of these expressions based on conditions, one falls into the views of either reification or denial.
Diverse establishments and diverse conceptualizations appear as various illusory conceptualizations.
Just as with various illusions, ordinary and ignorant sentient beings engage in diverse conceptualizations; this is not the case for the noble ones.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"Since those words are mere false imaginings, they establish all phenomena;
because of that establishment, one falls into the hells after death."
Within the aggregates there is no self, nor are the aggregates themselves the self;
it is not as those deluded ones imagine, yet it is also not that there is no self.
All things possess an intrinsic nature, yet it is like the delusions of the foolish and ignorant.
If things were as they are seen by them, then everyone should perceive the Truth.
All phenomena lack intrinsic nature; both purity and impurity do not exist at all.
They are unreal just as they are seen, yet they are not non-existent either.
"Furthermore, Mahāmati, I shall now explain the characteristics of gnosis (*jñāna*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*).
If you and the other bodhisattvas skillfully discern the characteristics of gnosis and consciousness, you will be able to penetrate their nature and swiftly attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
Mahāmati! That wisdom is of three kinds, namely:
worldly, supramundane, and the highest supramundane wisdom.
What is mundane knowledge?
It refers to all non-Buddhist practitioners and ordinary worldlings who cling to the notions of existence and non-existence.
What is supramundane wisdom?
It refers to all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas who fall into the expectation and attachment toward their own and common characteristics.
What is the supreme supramundane wisdom?

It refers to the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas who contemplate all dharmas as non-existent, perceive them as neither arising nor ceasing, transcend the categories of existence and non-existence, enter the stage of the Tathāgata, and give rise to self-realization through the non-self of persons and phenomena.
Mahāmati! That which arises and ceases is consciousness (*vijñāna*); that which neither arises nor ceases is wisdom (*jñāna*).

Furthermore, that which falls into the characteristics of the signless and into the various causal characteristics of existence and non-existence is consciousness; that which transcends the characteristics of existence and non-existence is wisdom.
Furthermore, that which has the characteristic of being nurtured is consciousness (*vijñāna*); that which does not have the characteristic of being nurtured is wisdom (*jñāna*).
Furthermore, there are three kinds of wisdom:
namely, knowing arising and ceasing, knowing specific and general characteristics, and knowing non-arising and non-ceasing.
Furthermore, the characteristic of non-obstruction is wisdom (*jñāna*).
The various obstructed characteristics of the objective sphere are consciousness (*vijñāna*).
Furthermore, the characteristic of the skillful means arising from the conjunction of the three factors is consciousness.
The characteristic of the intrinsic nature of the skillful means of non-activity is wisdom (*jñāna*).
Furthermore, the attainment of characteristics is consciousness (*vijñāna*);
the non-attainment of characteristics is wisdom.
"Having attained the realm of noble wisdom, one neither emerges nor enters; therefore, it is like the moon in water.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"The accumulation of karma constitutes consciousness; Non-accumulation constitutes wisdom."
Observing all phenomena, one penetrates their non-existence.
Attaining the power of mastery is what is called wisdom (*prajñā*);
binding to objective realms is the mind (*citta*), while the arising of awakened conceptualization is knowledge (*jñāna*).
From non-existence and excellence, wisdom is born;
mind, thought, and consciousness are far removed from conceptualization.
Having attained the state of non-conceptual dharma, such a one is a Son of the Buddha, not a Śrāvaka.
The patience of tranquil, supreme progress is the Tathāgata’s pure wisdom.
Born from the excellent ultimate truth, it is entirely free from all conditioned activity.
I possess three kinds of knowledge, which the Noble Ones have revealed as reality.
Contemplating those perceptions, one fully grasps all natures;
this is not compatible with the two vehicles, for wisdom is free from all that exists.
Clinging to intrinsic nature arises from the śrāvakas.
"Having transcended all mental constructs, the Tathāgata’s wisdom is pure.
"Furthermore, Mahāmati,
there are nine types of theories concerning transformation among the non-Buddhists."
The views of transformation arise among the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas), namely:

transformation of shape and location, transformation of characteristics, transformation of causes, transformation of completion, transformation of views, transformation of nature, transformation of the clarity of conditions, transformation of the clarity of actions, and transformation of things.
Mahāmati! These are called the nine kinds of views regarding transformation.
It is because of these that all non-Buddhists give rise to theories concerning existence, non-existence, birth, and transformation.
What is the transformation of shape and location?
It refers to the perception of a different shape and location.
For example, when gold is transformed into various vessels, diverse shapes and forms appear, yet the nature of the gold does not change.
The transformation of all natures is likewise so.

There may be non-Buddhists who form such false imaginings, even up to the false imagining of the transformation of things; these are neither identical nor different, because they are merely false imaginings.
In this way, one should understand that the transformation of all natures is like the ripening of milk, curd, wine, fruit, and so forth.

The non-Buddhists (tīrthika) have the false imagination of transformation, yet for them there is no such transformation. Whether existent or non-existent, it is a manifestation of one's own mind; external natures have no intrinsic reality.
Mahāmati!
In this way, foolish ordinary beings arise from the habitual cultivation of their own false imaginings. Mahāmati!
There is no dharma that arises or ceases, just as one perceives the arising of forms in a magical illusion or a dream.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
“Form, location, and temporal transformation; The four great elements and the sense faculties;
The intermediate state arises in succession— These are false imaginings, not the wisdom of the enlightened.”
“The Supreme One regarding dependent origination is not like those false imaginings;
rather, the dependent origination of the world is like a city of Gandharvas.
At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
We pray that you will explain for us the meaning of the continuity of all phenomena and the meaning of liberation.

If you skillfully distinguish between the characteristics of the continuity and non-continuity of all phenomena, we and the other bodhisattvas will well understand the skillful means regarding the continuity of all things, so as not to fall into attachment to continuity based on the literal meaning of what has been taught.”

He is skilled in the characteristics of the continuity and non-continuity of all phenomena, as well as in the awakening that transcends the conceptualization of words, letters, and speech; he travels through all Buddha-fields and immeasurable assemblies, possessing the seal of the power of mastery, supernormal knowledges, and dhāraṇīs, manifesting various transformations and radiating brilliant light.
With awakened wisdom, they skillfully enter the ten inexhaustible phrases and practice without expedient means.

Like the sun, moon, mani-jewel, and the four great elements, throughout all stages, they are free from the marks of their own deluded thoughts and views, seeing all phenomena as being like illusions, dreams, and so forth.

Entering the body of the Buddha-ground, he preaches the Dharma to all realms of sentient beings according to their needs and guides them, causing them all to dwell securely in the realization that all phenomena are like illusions, dreams, and so forth; free from the categories of existence and non-existence, as well as the delusions of arising and ceasing and the discrepancy between words and their meanings, his body becomes increasingly sublime.
The Buddha said to Mahāmati:
“Excellent, excellent!
Listen attentively, listen attentively!”
"Reflect upon this well; I shall speak for your sake.
Mahāmati said to the Buddha, "Yes, I shall receive your instruction."
The Buddha told Mahāmati:
"Regarding the infinite nature of all dharmas, there is a continuous attachment to the meanings as they have been explained.
That is to say:"

The continuity of attachment to signs; the continuity of attachment to conditions; the continuity of attachment to existence and non-existence; the continuity of attachment to the false discrimination of arising and non-arising; the continuity of attachment to the false discrimination of cessation and non-cessation; the continuity of attachment to the false discrimination of vehicles and non-vehicles; the continuity of attachment to the false discrimination of the conditioned and the unconditioned; the continuity of attachment to the false discrimination of the specific characteristics of each stage; the continuity of attachment to the uninterrupted false discrimination of one's own [subjective] delusions; the continuity of attachment to the false discrimination based on the dualistic categories of existence and non-existence held by outsiders; and the continuity of attachment to the uninterrupted false discrimination regarding the three vehicles and the one vehicle.
Furthermore, Mahāmati!
This and other ordinary, ignorant beings continue in the succession of their own false imaginings (*parikalpita*).

Because of this succession, the false imaginings of the ignorant are like a silkworm spinning its cocoon; they entangle themselves and others with the threads of false imagination, adhering to the characteristics of the succession of existence and non-existence.
Furthermore, Mahāmati! Within that state,
there is neither the characteristic of continuity nor the characteristic of non-continuity,
because one perceives all phenomena as quiescent and false conceptualization does not arise.
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas perceive all phenomena as quiescent.
Furthermore, Mahāmati,
they realize that external natures— whether existent or non-existent— are merely manifestations of their own minds and are ultimately non-existent.

By conforming to and observing that all things are merely the manifestations of one's own mind, and seeing that all natures—whether existent or non-existent—are signless, the continuity [of conceptualization] becomes tranquil; thus, regarding all phenomena, there is neither the characteristic of continuity nor the characteristic of discontinuity.
Furthermore, Mahāmati!
Within that [reality], there is neither bondage nor liberation.
Others, who fall into the error of not awakening to things as they truly are, perceive both bondage and liberation.
Why is this? It is because, regarding all phenomena, whether they exist or do not exist, no sentient being can be apprehended.
"Furthermore, Mahāmati!
Fools have three continuities, namely:
greed, hatred, and delusion, as well as craving for the future, accompanied by delight and lust.
Because of these continuities, there is the continuity of the realms of existence; that which continues is what continues within the five destinies.
Mahāmati! As for the severance of continuity, there is neither the characteristic of continuity nor the characteristic of non-continuity.
Furthermore, Mahāmati!
Through the condition of the conjunction of the three, one forms attachments through skillful means, and consciousness arises in uninterrupted succession.
Where there is attachment through skillful means, there is continuity.
When the consciousness conditioned by the conjunction of the three is severed and the three gates of liberation are seen, all continuity ceases to arise.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"Unreal conceptualization—this is said to be the characteristic of continuity.
If one knows its reality, the net of continuity is severed."
Lacking knowledge of all natures, they grasp at them according to verbal designations;
like silkworms that spin their own webs and entangle themselves,
the deluded are bound by false imaginings and fail to observe the continuity [of existence].
Mahāmati again addressed the Buddha, saying:

“As the World-Honored One has taught, by means of various conceptualizations, one conceptualizes various natures; yet those intrinsic natures do not exist, for they are merely the nature of conceptualization.”
Mahāmati said to the Buddha:
“World-Honored One,

if it is only the nature of false imagination and not the nature of intrinsic reality that exists in mutual dependence, would this not be a fault for the World-Honored One, as you have thus spoken of the non-existence of both affliction and purity?”
"All dharmas are of the nature of false imagination, because they lack intrinsic nature.
The Buddha told Mahāmati: "So it is, so it is!"
It is as you have said, Mahāmati!
It is not like the reality of the nature and self-nature of things as imagined by the ignorant.
This nature of imagined self-nature does not possess the characteristics of an existent self-nature. Mahāmati!
Just as there is an existent self-nature through noble wisdom—known by the noble ones, seen by the noble ones, and perceived by the noble eye of wisdom—in this way one knows the existent self-nature.
Mahāmati said to the Buddha:

"If it is as the noble ones do—knowing through the noble knowledge, seeing with the noble vision, and perceiving with the noble eye of wisdom, rather than with the divine eye or the fleshly eye—and thus knowing the self-nature of things as it truly is, unlike the false imaginings of foolish people;..."
"Bhagavān!
Why is it that foolish worldlings are separated from this false conceptualization and do not awaken to the reality of the noble nature?
Bhagavān!"
That, too, is neither inverted nor non-inverted. Why is this?
It is because:
Because they do not perceive the intrinsic nature of the reality of the noble ones, and because they do not see that which is free from the marks of existence and non-existence.
World-Honored One,
the noble ones likewise do not see in such a way, nor do they engage in such false conceptualization, for they do not take the realm of self-characteristics as their object.
"World-Honored One!

That too is the characteristic of the self-nature of things; such is the manifestation of the self-nature of conceptualization. It is not because of the absence of causes that it is so called, for that would entail falling into the view of [grasping at] the characteristics of self-nature."
It is a different realm, not like those [others], and thus there would be the fault of infinite regress.
World-Honored One!
