This is because they do not perceive the self-nature and characteristics of their own nature.
"World-Honored One!
Nor is it the nature of imagined self-nature, nor the characteristic of causal self-nature.
How is it that one knows, as they truly are, that which is imagined and that which is not imagined?"
"World-Honored One!
Conceptual construction is different, and the characteristic of self-nature is different.
World-Honored One!"
The cause is dissimilar, yet there is the conceptualization of the imagined nature.

Why is it that each [of these] is not conceptually constructed? Fools do not know this as it truly is; nevertheless, for the sake of causing sentient beings to abandon conceptual construction, I teach that the characteristics of conceptual construction do not exist as they truly are.
World-Honored One!

For what reason do you prohibit sentient beings from clinging to the self-nature of things through views of existence or non-existence, yet allow them to cling to the sphere of activity of noble wisdom by falling into the view of existence? You speak of the emptiness of dharmas as being without intrinsic nature, and yet you speak of the intrinsic nature of the reality of noble wisdom.
The Buddha told Mahāmati:

"It is not that I teach the dharma of emptiness as the absence of intrinsic nature (*asvabhāva*); nor do I fall into the view of existence by speaking of the reality of the self-nature of noble wisdom (*āryajñāna*). Rather, it is for the sake of causing sentient beings to abandon states of fear."

Since beginningless time, sentient beings have been attached to the characteristics of the intrinsic nature of things; they perceive the attachment to the characteristics of the intrinsic nature of the objects of noble wisdom, and thus I teach the Dharma of emptiness. Mahāmati!
I do not speak of the characteristics of the intrinsic nature of things,
Mahāmati! Rather,

I abide in the realization of the emptiness of dharmas as they truly are, free from the perceptions of delusive appearances, and free from the views of existence and non-existence regarding the manifestations of one's own mind.
Having attained the three liberations, they are sealed with the seal of reality as it is.
Regarding the self-nature of phenomena, they attain a dwelling in the observation of self-realized wisdom through conditions, free from the views and characteristics of existence and non-existence.
Furthermore, Mahāmati,
a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva should not establish the thesis that "all dharmas are unarisen. Why is this?
This means that because you maintain the thesis that all natures are non-natures, and because of the characteristic of being produced by those causes,
your thesis that "all dharmas are unproduced" is undermined. That thesis is undermined because your own thesis arises dependently.
Furthermore, that thesis of non-arising is undermined because it enters into all phenomena and because it does not destroy the characteristic of non-arising.
For one who establishes the thesis that all phenomena are unarisen, their own statement is thereby refuted.
Mahāmati!
The thesis that neither existence nor non-existence arises enters into all natures, for the characteristics of existence and non-existence cannot be apprehended therein,
Mahāmati!
If one were to establish a thesis based on the non-arising of all natures while simultaneously asserting that that very thesis does not arise, then that thesis would be undermined.
Since the characteristics of existence and non-existence do not arise, one should not establish a thesis.

Because the five-membered syllogism contains many fallacies, because its successive members possess distinct characteristics, and because it functions as a means of proof, one should not establish a thesis (*pakṣa*). That is to say, one should not establish a thesis such as "all phenomena are unarisen," nor likewise "all phenomena are empty," nor "all phenomena lack intrinsic nature" (*niḥsvabhāva*).
Mahāmati!

However, because Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas perceive that all phenomena manifest both appearing and non-appearing characteristics, and because they see the faults of [dualistic] views and cognitions, they should declare that all phenomena have the nature of being like illusions and dreams; except for the case where they speak of them as being like illusions and dreams merely to remove the state of fear in the minds of the ignorant.
"Mahāmati!
Fools fall into the views of existence and non-existence; do not cause them to become terrified and thereby abandon the Mahāyāna.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"Without intrinsic nature and without expression, without entities and without continuity—
these are the false imaginings of the foolish, like the evil perceptions of a corpse.
That all phenomena are unarisen is not the tenet of those non-Buddhists."
Ultimately there is nothing that arises; it is accomplished through the nature of conditions.
All phenomena are unarisen; the wise do not form conceptions of them.
Since their tenets arise from [causes], the Awakened One has completely eliminated them.
Just as one with cataracts sees the illusory appearance of falling hair, so too is the nature of conceptual attachment;
it is the false imagination of the foolish.
They designate the three realms of existence, yet there is no intrinsic nature to these phenomena.
The conceptualization of the self-nature of phenomena arises from discursive thought.
When signs and objects are established through verbal teachings, the mind becomes distracted and violently agitated;
yet the Son of the Buddha is able to transcend them and remain far removed from all such delusive imaginings.
What is not water is perceived as having the appearance of water; this arises from craving and thirst.
The deluded person is thus confused, but for the noble one, it is not so.
The noble one sees it as pure, born of the three liberations and samādhi.
Far removed from birth and death, they wander without fear.
Practicing the realization of non-existence, they perceive neither intrinsic nature nor the absence of nature;
through the equality of nature and its absence, the fruits of sainthood arise.
What is nature and what is non-nature?
What constitutes equality?
It is said that when the mind does not know, it is utterly tossed about within and without.
"If one can destroy that [duality], the mind will perceive with equanimity.
At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
As the Blessed One has said: "Just as when one grasps at an object, wisdom does not find it; this is a mere conventional designation, established by convention.
That which is grasped has no intrinsic nature, and the act of grasping likewise has no intrinsic nature."
Because there is no grasping, cognition does not arise; it is merely a conventional designation.

World-Honored One, why is it that cognition does not apprehend [the object], due to the fact that one does not perceive the self-characteristics and common characteristics as being either different or non-different?
Is it because their individual and common characteristics, as well as the various natures and self-natures, are obscured that wisdom cannot apprehend them?
Or is it because they are obstructed by mountains, crags, rocky walls, earth, water, fire, and wind that wisdom cannot apprehend them?
"Is it because they are extremely distant or extremely near that wisdom cannot apprehend them?
Or is it because they are old, young, blind, or otherwise lack their faculties that wisdom cannot apprehend them?
World-Honored One!"
If one does not perceive whether self-characteristics and common characteristics are different or non-different, and thus cognition does not apprehend them;
then one should not speak of "cognition," but rather of "non-cognition," because the object of apprehension is not found.

Furthermore, World-Honored One, if wisdom cannot apprehend various individual and common characteristics because their intrinsic natures and characteristics are obscured, then that is itself a lack of wisdom; it is not true wisdom.
World-Honored One!
Because there is an object (*ālambana*), knowledge arises; it is not that knowledge exists without encountering an object, and for this reason it is called "knowledge.

If, however, one does not perceive something—whether it be a mountain, a rock, a wall, earth, water, fire, or wind; whether it be extremely distant or extremely near; or if one is old, young, blind, ignorant, or lacks the sensory faculties—then this is also not knowledge.
It should rather be called "non-knowledge," because there is an existing thing that cannot be apprehended.
The Buddha told Mahāmati: "It is not so.
What is non-intelligence should be intelligence; it is not non-intelligence.
I do not conceal the fact that when one does not attain wisdom regarding the objects of perception, this is established as the measure of conceptual designation."

Having realized that what appears to one's own mind is merely a mental representation, and that existence and non-existence—whether external entities or their absence—are not to be found through cognition, such cognition does not arise toward the *tathatā* (suchness) because nothing is to be apprehended.
Because nothing is apprehended, cognition does not arise regarding the *dharmadhātu*.
In accordance with the three liberations, even wisdom cannot be apprehended.
That which is not conceptual construction is the beginningless nature and non-nature; it is through the habitual wisdom of falsehood that one forms such a cognition.
Thus, they know this but do not know that.
Consequently, regarding external objects and their locations, they treat their characteristics and natures as being without nature; thus, their false conceptualizations (vikalpa) are never severed.
Establishing what is merely the manifestation of their own minds, they speak of the marks of "I" and "mine," and remain attached through grasping.
Failing to realize that [the world] is the manifestation of one's own mind, one gives rise to false conceptualization regarding the objects of cognition (*jñeyaviṣaya*).
Because of this false conceptualization, one fails to perceive external natures as being either existent or non-existent, and thus falls into the view of nihilism.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"When there are objects of attachment, If wisdom does not examine them, This is ignorance, not true knowledge; So say those who harbor false imaginings."
When wisdom does not discern the nature of non-differentiation,
nor [discern] obstructions, distance, or proximity, this is called false wisdom.
When the faculties of the old and the young are obscured, wisdom does not arise.
Yet, that there actually exists such an appearance is also called false wisdom.

Furthermore, Mahāmati, foolish ordinary people are turned around by beginningless, false, evil, and perverse conceptualizations; while being thus turned around, they do not properly understand the thorough realization of one's own school (*svapratyātma-gati*) or the communication of the teaching (*deśanā-gati*).

"Because they are attached to the appearance of external objects as manifestations of their own minds, and because they are attached to expedient teachings, they do not skillfully discern the pure, universal characteristics of the four propositions within our own school.
Mahāmati said to the Buddha,
"It is exactly as you have taught, World-Honored One."
I only pray, World-Honored One,
that you will analyze and explain for me the *sūtra-vehicle* (the common teaching) and the *principle-vehicle* (the ultimate teaching).
May I and the other Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas become proficient in these two vehicles, so that in future ages ordinary people, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas shall find no fault in us.
The Buddha said to Mahāmati:
"Excellent, excellent!
Listen attentively, listen attentively!"
"Reflect upon this well; I shall speak for your sake.
Mahāmati said to the Buddha, "So be it;
I shall receive your instruction."
The Buddha told Mahāmati:
"The Tathāgatas of the three periods of time possess two kinds of dharma-attainments:
namely, the attainment of the teaching (deśanā-prativedha) and the attainment of one's own school (svaprakriyā-prativedha)."
As for the penetration of teaching, it means:
according to what is appropriate for the minds of sentient beings, one preaches various kinds of sūtras as necessary equipment.
This is called the penetration of teaching.
As for the penetration of one's own school (svapratyātmagatigocara),
it refers to the practitioner who is free from the various conceptual constructions manifested by their own mind.
That is to say:
It does not fall into the categories of identity, difference, both, or neither; it transcends all mind, intellect, and consciousness.

It is the self-realized realm of the sages, free from the characteristics of views formed by causes, and is unknowable to any non-Buddhists, śrāvakas, or pratyekabuddhas who have fallen into the two extremes.
I call this the dharma of the realization of one’s own school.
Mahāmati! These are called the characteristics of the realization of one’s own school and the communication through teaching.
"You and the other bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should practice and study this.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"My two kinds of penetration— The penetration of the principle and the penetration of verbal expression—"
"The expositor [teaches] the ignorant, while the essential principle is for the practitioner.
At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
As the Blessed One once said:
"Regarding the various discourses and arguments of the world, you must be careful not to associate with them.
If you do associate with them, you will embrace desire and fail to embrace the Dharma."
“World-Honored One, for what reason do you speak thus?
The Buddha told Mahāmati:
“Worldly discourse consists of various phrases and expressions, embellished by the study of causes, conditions, and parables; it is used to entice and delude foolish, ordinary people.”
Failing to enter into the true realization of their own nature, they do not awaken to all phenomena; through deluded and inverted thoughts, they fall into the two extremes.

Being foolish, ignorant, and confused, they bring about their own ruin; as they continue in the succession of various realms of existence, they fail to attain liberation. Unable to realize that things are merely manifestations of their own minds, they do not depart from external natures and essences, persisting in their deluded attachments.

Therefore, Mahāmati, the various discourses and eloquent explanations of worldly talk do not transcend birth, old age, sickness, death, grief, lamentation, suffering, and affliction; they are deceptive, delusive, and confusing.
Mahāmati!
Śakra Devānām Indra was widely learned in various treatises and had himself composed a work on phonology (*śabda-śāstra*).

A disciple of that Lokāyatika philosopher, assuming the form of a dragon, went to Śakra’s celestial palace to establish his own philosophical tenets, intending to destroy Śakra’s thousand-spoked wheel.
"If I am defeated, I shall cut off one head for each [of your defeats] to apologize for my submission.
Having made this vow, he then used the Dharma of Śiva to subdue Śakra.
Having explained the points of defeat, he destroys their wheel and returns to the human realm.

Thus, Mahāmati, worldly discourse, adorned with causes and analogies, can even cause animals to be deluded by various phrases and expressions, leading them—along with the gods and asuras—to become attached to views of arising and ceasing; how much more so for humans?
Therefore, Mahāmati, you should distance yourself from worldly discourse, for it brings about the causes for the arising of suffering; be careful not to cultivate or frequent it.
Mahāmati! Those who propound worldly treatises speak only of the realm of bodily perception. Mahāmati!
Those proponents of worldly doctrines number in the hundreds of thousands; however, in the future, during the final five hundred years, they shall destroy the communal recitation (saṃgīti).
Because false awakening and [wrong] views will flourish, evil disciples shall accept them.
In this way, Mahāmati, the worldly treatises destroy the [true] compilation;

they consist of various phrases and expressions adorned with causes and similes, which speak of the matters of non-Buddhists, clinging to their own causal conditions and lacking any self-attained realization.
Mahāmati!

Those various non-Buddhists lack a doctrine of their own; regarding other worldly treatises, they extensively expound upon immeasurable hundreds of thousands of categories of phenomena, yet they possess no doctrine of their own, nor do they realize that these are merely the foolish worldly treatises of their ignorance.
At that time, Mahāmati said to the Buddha:
"World-Honored One!

If the worldly discourses of the non-Buddhists, adorned with various phrases, expressions, causes, and analogies, lack any self-attained realization and are merely attachments to their own particular objects;..."

The World-Honored One also expounded upon worldly discourse, extensively explaining immeasurable varieties of phrases and expressions for the sake of the diverse assemblies of devas, humans, and asuras who had gathered from various regions.
"Is it not also your own established doctrine?
Does it not also fall within the category of the wisdom and discourse of all non-Buddhists?
The Buddha told Mahāmati:
“I do not speak of worldly discourse, nor is there coming or going; I speak only of neither coming nor going.
Mahāmati! ‘Coming’ refers to the gathering together that gives rise to birth.”
That which departs is dispersed and destroyed.
That which neither comes nor goes is neither born nor extinguished.
What I have taught does not fall within the categories of worldly discourse or deluded conceptualization.
Why is this so? It is because that which is not conceptualized consists of external natures and non-natures, which are merely the locus of what is manifested by one's own mind.
It cannot be overturned by the false imaginings of the two extremes.

When one realizes that the nature of objective marks is non-existent and perceives them as the manifestation of one’s own mind, then these manifestations of one’s own mind no longer give rise to false imaginings.
When false imaginings do not arise, there is emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; entering these three gates of liberation is called emancipation.
Mahāmati! I recall that at one time, while I was dwelling in a certain place,
a world-theorist brahmin came to visit me.
Without being invited to do so, he immediately asked me:
"Gautama! Is everything created?"
I then replied: "Brāhmaṇa!
All that has been done constitutes the first worldly doctrine."
He asked again: "Is everything uncreated? I replied:
"Everything is uncreated; this is the second worldly doctrine.
He then asked again:
"Is everything eternal?"
Are all things impermanent?
Are all things born?
Or are all things unborn?
I then replied:
"This is the doctrine of the six heretical teachers. Mahāmati!
He further asked me:
"Are all things one?
Or are all things different?"
Are all things simultaneous?
Are all things not simultaneous?
Do all things manifest through birth based on various causes?
I then replied:
"These are the eleven types of world-theorists. Mahāmati!
He asked again:
"Are all things indeterminate?
Or are all things determinate?"
Is there a self?
Is there no self?
Does this world exist?
Is there no present world?
Is there a future world?
Or is there no future world?
Is there liberation?
Is there no liberation?
Are all things momentary?
Are all things non-momentary?
Are they space?
Or are they analytical cessation?
"Nirvana? Gautama! Is it something created?"
Is it unconditioned?
Is there an intermediate state (antarābhava),
or is there no intermediate state?
"O Mahāmati! I then replied to him, 'Brāhmaṇa!'"
Such teachings as these are all merely worldly discourse (*lokāyata*).
They are not my teaching; they are your worldly discourse.

I teach only that beginningless, false, and delusive habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) give rise to various evils, which are the cause of the three realms of existence (*trai-dhātuka*). Failing to realize that all is a manifestation of one's own mind, one gives rise to delusive thoughts and clings to external objects.
“Brahmin, as it is in the teachings of the non-Buddhists— that the meaning of my sense faculties arises from the conjunction of the three—
I do not hold such a view. I do not speak of a cause, nor do I speak of no cause.”

I speak only of the nature of the grasped and the grasper as being comprised within false imagination, and I establish dependent origination; this is not something you can reach, nor can it be realized by others who have fallen into the continuity of the self-grasping notion.
“Mahāmati! Nirvāṇa, space, and cessation are not three distinct entities; there are simply three numerical designations.
Furthermore, Mahāmati!”
At that time, the Lokāyatika brāhmaṇa again asked me:
"Is the existence of the three realms of existence caused by ignorance, craving, and karma,
or is it without cause?"
I then replied: "These two are also merely worldly doctrines. He asked again:
"Are all natures included within their own and common characteristics?
I replied again: "This, too, is worldly discourse."
“O Brahmin! Even the mental stream’s false conceptualization of external objects is all worldly discourse.
Furthermore, Mahāmati:
At that time, the Lokāyatika Brahmin again asked me:
"Is there anyone who is not a proponent of worldly discourse?
I am the master of all non-Buddhist paths, expounding various phrases, flavors, causes, conditions, and adorned with parables."
I replied again:
"Brahmin! There is that which does not belong to you."

"It is not a worldly discourse, not a non-doctrine, not a non-exposition, yet it is not that various phrases and expressions are not expounded; it is not that it is not adorned with causes and analogies.
The brāhmaṇa asked:
"What is this which is not a worldly discourse, not a non-doctrine, and not a non-exposition?"
I then replied: "Brahmin!

There is a teaching that is not of worldly discourse, which you followers of external paths cannot know, because of your false attachment to the unreal, delusory constructions regarding external natures."
This means that when false conceptualization does not arise, one realizes that existence and non-existence are merely the manifestations of one's own mind.
When false conceptualization does not arise, one no longer receives external objects.
When false conceptualization is forever stilled, this is called "non-worldly discourse."
"This is my Dharma, not yours, O brāhmaṇa!
To speak briefly of that consciousness: it has various characteristics—whether coming or going, dying or being born, pleasure or pain, sinking or seeing, contact or attachment."
Whether it be through the combination of conditions, their continuity, sensation, or attachment to causes—O Brahmin!
Such things as these belong to your worldly doctrines; they are not mine.
"Mahāmati! When the world-discussing Brahmins asked such questions, I answered them in this way.
They then remained silent and withdrew without further protest."
Reflecting upon his own sphere of realization, he thought to himself:

"The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, have strayed outside of realized knowledge; they preach non-arising, signlessness, and causelessness, claiming that what appears is merely one's own deluded imagination, and that when this deluded imagination does not arise, [liberation is attained]."
"Mahāmati! This is precisely what you asked me just now:

'For what reason do you say that associating with those who debate worldly treatises and engaging in various forms of sophistry leads to the grasping of desire, and not to the grasping of the Dharma?'"
Mahāmati said to the Buddha:
“World-Honored One,
what is the meaning of the phrases regarding the grasping of desire and the grasping of dharmas?”
The Buddha said to Mahāmati:
"Excellent, excellent!
You are indeed able, for the sake of future sentient beings, to contemplate and inquire about the meaning of such phrases."
"Listen attentively, listen attentively!
Reflect upon it well; I shall speak for your sake.
Mahāmati said to the Buddha:
“Very well, we shall receive your instruction.
The Buddha told Mahāmati:
“What is called ‘craving’ refers to grasping, rejecting, touching, or savoring; it is being bound by and attached to external objects, thereby falling into the views of the two extremes.”
Furthermore, the aggregate of suffering arises: birth, old age, sickness, death, grief, lamentation, pain, and distress.
All such afflictions originate from craving; this results from associating with worldly discourse and those who engage in worldly discourse. I and all the Buddhas declare this to be greed.
This is called embracing desire and not embracing the Dharma.
Mahāmati, what is meant by embracing the Dharma?

That is to say: it is the skillful realization that all is but the manifestation of one’s own mind; seeing the marks of both the selflessness of persons and the selflessness of phenomena, so that false conceptualization no longer arises;

skillfully knowing the lower and upper stages (*bhūmi*); being free from mind, thought, and consciousness (*citta-mano-manovijñāna*); receiving the empowerment (*abhiṣeka*) of the wisdom of all Buddhas; fully embracing the ten inexhaustible phrases; and attaining mastery over all phenomena without effort—this is called the Dharma.
That is to say, Mahāmati, it is not falling into any views, any pretenses, any conceptual constructions, any natures, or any two extremes.
Mahāmati!
There are many foolish followers of external paths who fall into the two extremes of eternalism or nihilism; they are not wise people.
By accepting the doctrine of no-cause, they give rise to the view of permanence;
by claiming that external causes and the destruction of conditions lack intrinsic nature, they give rise to the view of annihilation.
"Mahāmati!
Because I do not perceive arising, abiding, or ceasing, I designate it as 'Dharma.
Mahāmati!"
"This is called desire and the Dharma.
You and the other bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should practice and study this.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"All worldly treatises are the false doctrines of outsiders;
through their deluded views, they posit both creator and created, yet they possess no system of their own.
Only I have my own system, which is free from both creator and created."
For the sake of his disciples, he taught them to remain far removed from all worldly treatises.
The mind-only is invisible; one does not observe two minds.
Since the grasped and the grasper lack intrinsic nature, one is free from both extremes of annihilation and permanence.
As long as the mind continues to flow, this is merely worldly discourse.
When false conceptualization no longer turns, such a person perceives their own mind:
that which "comes" is called the arising of phenomena, and that which "goes" is the non-appearance of phenomena.
Clearly understanding the past and the future, Delusive thoughts no longer arise.
Regarding permanence and impermanence, The conditioned and the unconditioned,
This world and the world beyond— All such matters are encompassed by worldly discourse.
At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Regarding what is called ‘nirvāṇa,’ of what kind of dharma is it that is named nirvāṇa?”
"Yet the various non-Buddhists each give rise to their own deluded imaginings.
The Buddha told Mahāmati:
"Listen attentively, listen attentively!"
"Reflect upon this well; I shall explain it for you.
The nirvana imagined by the various non-Buddhists is not a nirvana that accords with their own conceptualizations.
Mahāmati said to the Buddha:
“Very well, we shall receive your instruction.
The Buddha told Mahāmati:

“There are some non-Buddhists who [assert that] the cessation of the aggregates (skandhas), elements (dhātus), and sense-bases (āyatanas), the detachment from sense objects, and the vision of the impermanence of phenomena lead to the non-arising of the categories of mind and mental factors. They do not contemplate objects of the past, future, or present; all sensations and aggregates are exhausted like the extinguishing of a lamp or the destruction of a seed, such that false conceptualization no longer arises.”
These people form the notion of nirvāṇa regarding this. Mahāmati,
it is not by the destruction of views that one is said to have attained nirvāṇa.
Mahāmati! Some consider liberation to be the transition from one direction to another, wherein the conceptualization of objective realms ceases, just as the wind subsides.
Others, again, consider liberation to be the destruction of the perception of the knower and the known.
Some perceive permanence and impermanence, conceiving them as liberation.
Others perceive various marks and notions, which bring about the causes for the arising of suffering;

having reflected on this, they fail to correctly discern that these are merely the manifestations of their own minds. Fearing these marks, they perceive the markless and develop a deep attachment to it, conceiving it to be nirvana.

Some perceive that all internal and external phenomena—whether characterized by specific or general marks, and whether past, future, or present—possess an indestructible intrinsic nature, and thus conceive of this as nirvana.
Others maintain that the self, the person, sentient beings, and the life-span, as well as all phenomena, undergo total destruction, and thus conceive of this as nirvana.

Or, because non-Buddhists have scorched their wisdom with evil views, they perceive both primordial nature (*prakṛti*) and the person (*puruṣa*); they see that these two are distinct, and that which is produced by the person is called primordial nature.
Just as in the analogy of primordial darkness, they conceive of the transformation of *guṇa* (qualities); they regard *guṇa* as the agent and imagine it to be *nirvāṇa*.
Some say it is the exhaustion of merit and demerit; some say it is the exhaustion of all afflictions; others say it is wisdom.
Some perceive Īśvara as the true creator of birth and death, conceiving of him as Nirvāṇa;
others claim that birth and death arise through mutual succession, with no other cause.
Such [views] are precisely attachments to causes, yet those fools are unable to perceive this.
Because they do not know, they conceive the notion of nirvāṇa.
Some non-Buddhists say that by attaining the path of true reality, one conceives the notion of nirvāṇa.
Some perceive merit and the conjunction of that which arises from merit, and by regarding them as identical, different, both, or neither, they conceive the notion of nirvāṇa.

Others perceive the patterns on a peacock’s plumage arising from its own nature, as well as the natures of various mixed jewels, sharp thorns, and so forth; having seen these, they conceive the notion of nirvāṇa.

Mahāmati! Some perceive twenty-five principles; some are kings who protect their nations and, having studied the *Ṣaḍdharmapada* (Treatise on the Six Virtues), conceive the notion that this is nirvāṇa.
Others see time as the creator, and [perceive] the world as being subject to the seasons; those who perceive in such ways conceive the notion that this is nirvāṇa.

Some speak of "nature," some speak of "non-nature," some speak of knowing nature and non-nature, and some perceive a distinction between awakening and nirvana, forming the conceptualization of nirvana.
There are various such delusions as these, spoken by non-Buddhists, which fail to establish what they seek to establish and are rejected by the wise. Mahāmati,
all such things fall into the two extremes and are merely conceived as nirvāṇa.
Such are the false conceptions of nirvāṇa held by these non-Buddhists; within them, there is absolutely no arising or ceasing.
Mahāmati! Each of those various nirvāṇas of the non-Buddhists is merely according to their own treatises.
When observed with wisdom, nothing whatsoever is established.
Just as those deluded thoughts of the mind and intellect come and go, drifting, racing, and flowing, there is not a single one among them that attains nirvana.
Mahāmati!
Regarding what I have called "nirvāṇa," it refers to the thorough realization that all things are manifestations of one's own mind.
There are four kinds of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*): first, direct perception; second, inference; third, analogy; and fourth, authoritative tradition.

Those non-Buddhists fail to establish themselves within any of the four means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); they do not cling to external natures, they transcend the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*), and they perceive the state of reality as it is. They do not follow the dual extremes of false imagination manifested by their own minds, and they find that neither the grasping subject nor the grasped object can be apprehended.
All measurements fail to see what is established; being deluded regarding reality, one should not grasp at them.
Having abandoned those, one attains the noble Dharma of self-awakening.
Knowing the two kinds of selflessness, being free from the two kinds of afflictions, purifying the two obstructions, and forever transcending the two kinds of death;

on the successive higher stages and the stage of the Tathāgata, through profound samādhis such as those of shadows and illusions, which are free from mind, thought, and mentation—this is called nirvāṇa.
Mahāmati!
You and the other bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should practice and study this; you must swiftly distance yourselves from all views of nirvāṇa held by the various non-Buddhist paths.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
“The views of nirvāṇa held by the non-Buddhists Each arise from their own deluded imaginings;
Born from the mind’s conceptualizations, They lack the skillful means for liberation.”
The fool, bound by fetters, is far removed from skillful means;
with the notion of liberation held by non-Buddhists, liberation will never arise.
The various wisdoms of the many paths are common to the views of non-Buddhists.
They all lack liberation, because of their foolishness and false conceptualization.
All ignorant non-Buddhists falsely perceive agent and action;
they debate the categories of existence and non-existence, yet they all lack liberation.
The foolish delight in false conceptualization, And do not hear the wisdom of reality.
Verbal expressions are the root of the three sufferings; Reality is the cause for extinguishing suffering.
Just like an image in a mirror, Though it appears, it does not exist.
In the mirror of the deluded mind, the ignorant perceive duality.
Failing to recognize the mind and its objects, they give rise to two kinds of false conceptualization;
when the mind and its spheres are thoroughly understood, false conceptualization does not arise.
The mind itself is manifold; it is far removed from the signifier and the signified.
Though phenomena appear, they do not truly exist, just like the deluded imaginings of the ignorant.
The three realms of existence are merely imagination; external objects do not exist at all.
Various manifestations appear through false conceptualization, which the ignorant and foolish cannot comprehend.
Sūtra after sūtra explains that these are but false conceptualizations; ultimately, they do not transcend names.
If one were to depart from language, there would likewise be nothing to be expressed.

At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I only pray that you will explain the Samyaksaṃbuddha for me and for the other bodhisattva-mahāsattvas,
so that we may become skilled in the self-nature of the Tathāgata, awakening ourselves and awakening others.
The Buddha said to Mahāmati:
"Ask whatever you wish; I shall explain it to you according to your questions.
Mahāmati addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Is the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, a creator?
Or is he not a creator?”
Is it an effect? Is it a cause?
Or is it a characteristic?
Is it the characterized?
Is it the teaching?
Or is it that which is taught?
Is it the awakening?
Or is it that which is awakened to?
Regarding such phrases as these, are they different or not different?
The Buddha told Mahāmati:
"The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, regarding such phrases as these, is neither an entity nor a cause."
Why is this? Because both [positions] entail faults, Mahāmati.
If the Tathāgata were a conditioned phenomenon (*saṃskṛta*), he would be either produced or impermanent.
Because he would be impermanent, all conditioned phenomena would be the Tathāgata;
this is something neither I nor the Buddhas desire.
If it were not something created, then because nothing could be attained, skillful means would be empty—identical to a rabbit's horn or the son of a barren woman—since they do not exist at all.
Mahāmati! If there were neither object nor cause, then it would be neither existent nor non-existent.
If it were neither existent nor non-existent, it would transcend the four propositions.
The four propositions are worldly discourse.
That which transcends the four propositions does not fall into the four propositions.
Because it does not fall [into them], it is what the wise accept.
The meaning of the phrases of all Tathāgatas is likewise; the wise should understand this.
As I have taught—that all phenomena are without self—one should know that this meaning is that the nature of being without self is itself non-self.
All phenomena possess their own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and lack the intrinsic nature of others, just as in the case of oxen and horses.
Mahāmati! For example, it is not the case that the nature of an ox is the nature of a horse, nor that the nature of a horse is the nature of an ox.
In truth, they are neither existent nor non-existent; it is not that they lack their own specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*).

Thus, Mahāmati, all dharmas do not lack their own specific characteristics, yet they possess their own specific characteristics in a way that is not something that can be known by foolish worldlings who are ignorant of the absence of self (*anātman*).
Because of conceptual construction, all such phenomena are empty, unarisen, and without intrinsic nature.
One should understand it thus.
In this way, the Tathāgata is neither different from nor non-different from the aggregates.
If it were not different from the aggregates, it would be impermanent.
If it were different, then skillful means would be empty.
If both were the case, there would have to be a difference between them.
Just as the horns of an ox are not different because they resemble one another,
yet are different due to distinctions such as length and shortness,
so it is with all phenomena.
Mahāmati!
Just as the right horn of an ox is different from the left horn, and the left horn is different from the right horn, so too are length, shortness, and various colors each distinct from one another.
Mahāmati!
The Tathāgata is neither different from nor not different from the aggregates, elements, and sense bases.
In this same way, the liberation of the Tathāgata is neither different from nor not different [from them].
Thus, the Tathāgata is designated by the name "liberation."
If the Tathāgata were different from liberation, he would be constituted by material characteristics;
because he would be constituted by material characteristics, he would be impermanent.
If they were not different, then when a practitioner attains realization, there should be no differentiation, yet the practitioner perceives differentiation.
Therefore, they are neither different nor not different.
In this same way, wisdom and its cognitive objects are neither different nor not different, Mahāmati!

Wisdom and its manifestations are neither different nor not different; they are neither permanent nor impermanent; they are neither the agent nor the acted-upon; they are neither conditioned nor unconditioned; they are neither the perceiver nor the perceived; they are neither the characteristic nor the characterized; they are neither the aggregates nor distinct from the aggregates; they are neither the speaker nor the spoken; they are neither one nor different; they are neither both nor neither.

Because they are neither identical nor different, neither both nor neither, they are entirely free from all measures (*pramāṇa*). That which is called "measure" consists of seeing, hearing, cognizing, and knowing.
Being free from all measures, there is no verbal expression.
Where there is no verbal expression, there is no arising.
Where there is no arising, there is no ceasing.
Where there is no ceasing, there is quiescent extinction.
Quiescence is the nirvana of intrinsic nature.
The nirvana of intrinsic nature is without object and without cause.
Being without object and without cause, it is without objective support.
Without objective support (*anālambana*), one transcends all falsehood.
To transcend all falsehood is to be the Tathāgata.
The Tathāgata is the Samyaksaṃbuddha.
Mahāmati!
This is called Samyaksaṃbuddha.
A Buddha is one who is free from all faculties and measures.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"Completely free from the measures of the sense-faculties, Without objects and without causes,
Already free from the perceiver and the perceived, And also free from the characteristic and the characterized."
The aggregates and conditions are perfectly awakened; neither as one nor as different can they be seen.
If there is no seer, how could there be conceptual differentiation?
They are neither created nor uncreated, neither effect nor cause.
It is not the aggregates, nor does it reside within the aggregates;
it is neither something else nor a mixture, nor does it possess various natures, as is seen through false conceptualization.
One should know that it is also not non-existent; this is the very nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
Because of existence there is non-existence; because of non-existence there is existence.
If it were non-existent, one should not grasp it; if it were existent, one should not conceptualize it.
Whether regarding self or non-self, one remains entangled in the measures of verbal expression.
Immersed in the two extremes, they destroy themselves and ruin the world.
Liberated from all faults and possessing correct insight into the self, this is called right contemplation;
such a person does not disparage the Great Teacher.
At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
As the World-Honored One has said, the sūtras uphold the teaching of non-arising and non-ceasing.”
Furthermore, the World-Honored One has said that "non-arising and non-ceasing" is another name for the Tathāgata.
World-Honored One, why do you speak of non-arising and non-ceasing on account of the absence of intrinsic nature?
"Is this another name for the Tathāgata?
The Buddha told Mahāmati:
"I teach that all dharmas are neither arising nor ceasing; the categories of existence and non-existence do not appear."
Mahāmati said to the Buddha:
“World-Honored One!
If all dharmas are non-arising, then the apprehension of dharmas cannot be obtained, because all dharmas are non-arising.”
"If there is a dharma within names, I pray that you will explain it for me.
The Buddha told Mahāmati:
"Excellent, excellent!"
"Listen attentively!
Reflect upon it well; I shall analyze and explain it for you.
Mahāmati said to the Buddha:
“Very well, we shall receive your instruction.
The Buddha told Mahāmati:

“When I speak of the Tathāgata, it is not that he is without nature; nor is it that [the Tathāgata] encompasses all dharmas by being neither born nor extinguished; nor is it that he is neither born nor extinguished because he does not depend on conditions; nor is it that he is without meaning.”
Mahāmati!

What I call the name of the Tathāgata as the Mind-born Dharma-body is that which is unborn; it is not within the realm of any outsiders, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, or bodhisattvas of the seventh stage.
Mahāmati! That non-arising is a synonym for the Tathāgata. Mahāmati!
For example, Indra, Śakra, and Purandara—such things as these each have many names; yet, although they have many names, they do not possess multiple natures, nor are they devoid of intrinsic nature.
In this way, Mahāmati!

In this Sahā world—*Sahā* being translated as "Endurance"—I have three hundred thousand *asaṃkhyeya* names. Fools hear them all and each speaks of my name, yet they do not understand that these are different names for me, the Tathāgata.
Mahāmati! There are some sentient beings who know me as the Tathāgata; some who know me as the Omniscient One; some who know me as the Buddha;
some who know me as the Savior of the World; some who know me as the Self-Awakened One; and some who know me as the Guide.
There are those who know him as the Wide Guide, those who know him as the All-Guide, those who know him as the Rishi,
those who know him as Brahmā, those who know him as Viṣṇu, those who know him as Īśvara, those who know him as the Victorious One,
those who know him as Kapila, those who know him as the Limit of Reality, and those who know him as the Moon.
There are those who know the sun; there are those who know birth; there are those who know non-birth; there are those who know non-extinction;
there are those who know emptiness; there are those who know suchness; there are those who know the truths; there are those who know the limit of reality;
there are those who know the nature of phenomena; there are those who know nirvana; and there are those who know permanence.
There are those who know equality, those who know non-duality, those who know signlessness,
those who know liberation, those who know the Path, and those who know the mind-born.
Mahāmati!
These and other such names, numbering three hundred thousand asaṃkhyeyas, neither increase nor decrease.
In this world and in all other worlds, they all know me to be like the moon in water—neither emerging nor entering.
Those foolish people are unable to know me because they have fallen into the two extremes.

Nevertheless, they all pay me respectful homage and make offerings, yet they do not skillfully understand the meaning and intent of my words; they do not discern names, they do not comprehend self-evident principles, and they remain attached to various forms of speech and textual phrases.
Regarding that which is neither arising nor ceasing, they conceive of it as being without intrinsic nature.
They do not understand the distinctions among the names and titles of the Tathāgatas, such as Indra, Śakra, and Brahmā.
Failing to understand how to penetrate through to their own nature and reach the ultimate convergence,
they become attached to whatever is said regarding all phenomena. Mahāmati!
Those deluded people speak thus: "The meaning is identical to the expression;
the meaning and the expression are no different. Why is this so?"
This means that because meaning has no physical body, apart from verbal expression there is no further meaning; it is merely verbal expression itself.

Mahāmati! Those whose wisdom is corrupted by evil do not understand the self-nature of verbal expression, nor do they understand the arising and ceasing of verbal expression, whereas meaning neither arises nor ceases.
Mahāmati! All verbal expressions fall within the realm of letters, but the meaning does not so fall.
This is because it is free from both existence and non-existence; thus, there is no taking birth, nor is there any body.
Mahāmati!
The Tathāgata does not speak of dharmas that fall into words, because the existence or non-existence of words cannot be apprehended; this is excepting those [dharmas] that do not fall into words.
Mahāmati!
If anyone were to say that the Tathāgata teaches a dharma that falls within the realm of words and letters, this would be a false statement;
for the Dharma is free from words and letters. Therefore, Mahāmati!
We Buddhas and Bodhisattvas do not speak a single word, nor do we answer with a single word.
Why is this? Because the Dharma is free from words and letters.
It is not that these teachings do not have the purpose of benefiting others;
rather, they are called "discourse" because sentient beings are characterized by false conceptualization, Mahāmati.
If all dharmas were not taught, the teaching would perish.
If the teaching perishes, then there would be no Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Pratyekabuddhas, or Śrāvakas.
If there were nothing [existent], for whom would anyone speak?
Therefore, Mahāmati,
let bodhisattva-mahāsattvas not cling to verbal expression, but rather expound the Dharma extensively through skillful means as appropriate to the occasion.

Because the hopes and afflictions of sentient beings are not uniform, I and the various Buddhas teach the various dharmas for those beings of diverse understandings, so that they may leave behind mind, intellect, and consciousness; it is not for the sake of attaining the state of self-realized noble wisdom.
Mahāmati!
Regarding all phenomena as non-existent, one awakens to the manifestation of one's own mind and leaves behind the two kinds of false conceptualization.
All Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas rely on the meaning, not on the words.
If good sons or good daughters rely on the literal words, they will destroy the ultimate truth for themselves and will be unable to awaken others.

Falling into a continuous succession of wrong views, they will preach to the assembly while failing to properly understand all dharmas, all stages, and all characteristics, nor will they understand the chapters and phrases.

If one is skilled in all dharmas, all stages, and all characteristics, has mastered the words and phrases, and is fully endowed with the meaning of their nature, then that person can delight in the true joy of signlessness and establish sentient beings in the equal Mahāyāna.
Mahāmati!
To embrace the Mahāyāna is to embrace all Buddhas, bodhisattvas, pratyekabuddhas, and śrāvakas.
To embrace all Buddhas, bodhisattvas, pratyekabuddhas, and śrāvakas is to embrace all sentient beings.
To embrace all sentient beings is to embrace the true Dharma.
To embrace the true Dharma is to ensure that the lineage of the Buddhas is not severed.
When the lineage of the Buddhas is not severed, one is able to thoroughly understand and attain the sublime state of entry.
Knowing the sublime points of entry, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva always attains transformation birth and establishes the Mahāyāna.
Through the power of the ten masteries, they manifest various forms and images.
He penetrates the various forms, inclinations, and afflictions of sentient beings and teaches the Dharma according to reality.
"According to reality" means it is not otherwise.
"According to reality" means it is a state without coming or going, wherein all falsehoods have ceased.
This is called "as-it-is. Mahāmati!
Sons and daughters of good family should not grasp at or adhere to discursive explanations.
Reality is that which is free from words.
Mahāmati, it is like using a finger to point at an object for a fool; the fool gazes at the finger and fails to grasp the actual meaning.

In this way, such foolish people follow the pointing finger of verbal expression, grasping at it and becoming attached to it, never relinquishing it until the end; thus, they are ultimately unable to attain the supreme ultimate truth that transcends the pointing finger of verbal expression.
Mahāmati!
It is like an infant who should eat cooked food and not raw food;
if he were to eat raw food, it would cause him to go mad.
Because they do not know how to ripen [the mind] through the sequential methods. Mahāmati!
Thus, this non-arising and non-ceasing, if not cultivated through skillful means, is unwholesome.
Therefore, you should skillfully cultivate expedient means and not follow mere words, just as one who looks at the tip of a finger [misses the moon].
For this reason, Mahāmati,
you should skillfully cultivate practice regarding the ultimate reality.
The true meaning is subtle and tranquil; it is the cause of nirvana.
Discursive speech is conjoined with false conceptualization.
False conceptualization accumulates birth and death.
"Mahāmati!
True meaning is obtained from those who have heard much.
Mahāmati!"
One who is "learned" (bahuśruta) refers to one who is skilled in meaning, not merely skilled in verbal expression.

One who is skilled in meaning does not follow any of the scriptures or treatises of the non-Buddhists; neither following them oneself nor causing others to follow them—this is what is called being a virtuous person of great learning.

Therefore, those who wish to seek the meaning should associate with those who are learned; that which is called "good meaning" is what one should associate with through learning. That which is called "good meaning" is indeed what one should associate with through learning.
"Contrary to this, one should distance oneself from attachment to verbal expressions.
At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva, further empowered by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual authority, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
The World-Honored One’s revelation of non-arising and non-ceasing is nothing extraordinary. Why is this?
For the causes of all external paths are likewise neither arising nor ceasing.
The World-Honored One has also spoken of space, non-analytical cessation, analytical cessation, and the realm of nirvana as being neither arising nor ceasing.
World-Honored One,
the non-Buddhists speak of causes that give rise to all worlds.
The World-Honored One has also taught that ignorance, craving, karma, and false conceptualization serve as conditions for the arising of all worlds.
These are merely different names for these causes and conditions; the same applies to the causes and conditions of external objects.
"So it is, World-Honored One!
There would be no distinction from the treatises of the non-Buddhists.
[They claim that] the nine substances—such as atoms, the supreme spirit (pradhāna), the sovereign lord (īśvara), and the lord of sentient beings—are neither born nor extinguished."
The World-Honored One also teaches that all natures are neither born nor extinguished, and that existence and non-existence cannot be apprehended.
The heterodox teachers likewise teach that the four great elements are indestructible and that their intrinsic nature is neither born nor extinguished.
The four great elements are eternal;
these four great elements, even as they circulate through the various realms of existence, do not abandon their own nature.
What the World-Honored One has taught is likewise so.
Therefore, I say that there is nothing extraordinary about this.
I only pray that the World-Honored One will explain the distinctions by which it is extraordinary and superior to all other heterodox paths.
If there were no such distinctions, then all heterodox teachers would likewise be Buddhas.
Because they are neither born nor extinguished, the World-Honored One has said that it is impossible for many Buddhas to appear in a single world-system.
Yet, as previously stated, there should be many Buddhas in a single world-system, because there would be no distinction between them.
The Buddha told Mahāmati:
"My teaching of non-arising and non-ceasing is not the same as the non-arising and non-ceasing of the non-Buddhists. Why is this so?"
Those various non-Buddhists maintain that there is a self-nature (*svabhāva*) which possesses the characteristics of being unarisen and immutable.
I do not fall into such positions of existence or non-existence, Mahāmati.
The self is free from the categories of existence and non-existence, and is devoid of arising and ceasing; it is neither a nature nor a lack of nature.
Because it manifests like various illusions and dreams, it is not without nature.
Why is it not without nature?
This means that form is encompassed by the characteristic of selflessness, because it appears and does not appear, and because it is grasped and not grasped.

For this reason, all natures are neither existent nor non-existent; rather, when one realizes that they are merely the manifestation of one's own mind, deluded thoughts do not arise, and there is peace, happiness, and the eternal cessation of worldly affairs.
Ignorant ordinary beings engage in activities based on false conceptualization, whereas the noble ones do not.
These unreal conceptualizations are like a city of the Gandharvas or a magically conjured person.
Mahāmati! It is like a city of the Gandharvas or a conjured illusion, where various beings appear to come and go as merchants.
Fools, through their false imaginings, believe there is real coming and going; yet in reality, there is no one who comes or goes, for it is merely due to their false imaginings.
In this way, Mahāmati!
Foolish ordinary people give rise to the notions of non-arising and non-ceasing; yet for them, there is neither the conditioned nor the unconditioned.
It is like the birth of an illusory person: in reality, there is neither arising nor ceasing, because both existence and non-existence are non-existent.
All phenomena are likewise thus, free from arising and ceasing.
Foolish ordinary beings, falling into what is unreal, give rise to the false discrimination of arising and ceasing; this is not the case for the noble sages.
It is not as it appears to those who do not see reality as it is;
for it is not otherwise than the imagined nature of self-nature.
If it were different from the imagined nature, one would be attached to all self-natures and would not perceive tranquility.
Those who do not perceive tranquility will never be free from conceptual construction.
Therefore, Mahāmati,
the vision of signlessness is superior.
That which is not seeing characteristics as characteristics is the cause for the arising of rebirth; therefore, it is not supreme. Mahāmati!
That which is signless is the non-arising of false discrimination; it neither arises nor ceases—this I call nirvāṇa.
Mahāmati!

As for nirvāṇa, it is the vision of the true meaning, which is free from the previously existing conceptualizations of mind and mental factors; having attained the noble wisdom of the Tathāgata’s self-realization, I call this nirvāṇa.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
“Having eliminated the theories of arising, I establish the principle of non-arising;
Though I preach such a Dharma, The foolish are unable to understand it.”
All phenomena are unarisen; they lack intrinsic nature and are non-existent.
Like a gandharva-city, a magical illusion, or a dream, that which possesses intrinsic nature has no cause.
Since there is no arising and no intrinsic nature, for what reason should emptiness be explained?
Because when separated from their combination, the nature of cognition does not manifest, emptiness is non-arising;
therefore, I teach that they lack intrinsic nature.
When each individual element is combined, the nature appears, yet it does not exist.
Upon analysis, there is no combination; it is not as the non-Buddhists perceive.
Like dreams, illusions, and falling hairs, like mirages and gandharva cities, the various phenomena of the world appear without a cause.
He subdues those who propound causalism and elucidates the meaning of non-arising.
In elucidating non-arising, he ensures that the stream of the Dharma flows forever without interruption;
by fiercely burning away theories of causelessness, he strikes terror into all non-Buddhists.
What is it? What is its cause? For what reason does it arise?
In what place do its factors combine? Why do you propound the doctrine of causelessness?
Upon examining conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*), one finds they are neither causeless nor possess a [single] cause.
For those who propound the theory of arising and ceasing, what they perceive is thereby extinguished.
What is meant by "non-arising"? Is it the absence of intrinsic nature?
Or is it that, in view of all conditions, there is a phenomenon called "non-arising"?
Names should not be without meaning; they are taught solely for the sake of conceptual differentiation.
It is not that there is no nature or no arising, nor is it that names depend upon various conditions.
It is not that names exist because of an inherent nature, yet names are also not without meaning.
All heterodox teachers, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas—this is not the domain of those up to the seventh stage;
this is called the characteristic of non-arising.
It is far removed from all causes and conditions, and likewise free from all phenomena.
Only the subtle mind abides; when both the perceiver and the perceived are abandoned, the body undergoes transformation—this I call non-arising.
There is no external nature nor the absence of nature, nor is there any grasping by the mind.
The severing of all views—this I call non-arising.
Such is the absence of intrinsic nature; emptiness and the like should be distinguished accordingly.
It is not because things are empty that they are called "empty," but because they are unarisen that they are called "empty."
Through the combination of causes and conditions, there is arising and ceasing;
apart from these causes and conditions, there is no separate arising or ceasing.
Apart from the combination of causes and conditions, there is no other distinct nature.
To speak of identity or difference is the false conceptualization of the non-Buddhists.
Since the nature of existence and non-existence does not arise, it is neither existent nor non-existent;
apart from the transformations of numerical categories, none of these can be apprehended.
There are only various conventional designations, Linked together in a chain of mutual dependence;
Apart from that chain of causes and conditions, The meaning of "arising" cannot be found.
Since arising lacks intrinsic nature, it does not occur, And thus one is free from the errors of the non-Buddhists.
I speak only of dependent origination as a chain; the foolish and ignorant cannot comprehend it.
If there were a nature of arising existing apart from this chain of dependent origination, that would be a doctrine of causelessness, which destroys the meaning of the chain.
Just as a lamp reveals various forms, so do the links of dependent origination appear;
yet if they were separate from these links, there would be other natures.
Since there is no nature, there is no arising, for their intrinsic nature is like that of space.
If one is free from the chain of causal links, wisdom has nothing to differentiate.
Furthermore, there is another aspect of non-arising: the dharma attained by the noble ones.

Regarding that which arises and that which does not arise—where "that which arises" refers to the arising of the four marks—this is precisely the patience regarding non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*).
One who observes the chain of causal links finds that all things are free from such links;
from this, one attains samādhi.
This is the internal chain of links: the fire-drill, the flint, the lump of clay, and the potter’s wheel.
If seeds and the like are called "external" yet arise from causes and conditions, they do not possess the meaning of a causal chain;
thus, [the doctrine] is not established.
If that which arises lacks intrinsic nature, for whom would it serve as a causal chain?
Since things arise through mutual succession, one should understand this as the meaning of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
That which arises from causes and conditions does not possess the meaning of a causal chain.
This would then be unestablished.
The ignorant give rise to false imaginings; apart from enumeration, there is no distinct phenomenon—this is what is meant by "the absence of intrinsic nature."
There is no multiplicity of doctrines; rather, because diseases differ, various treatments are prescribed.
To destroy all afflictions, one must know the superior or inferior nature of their roots.
For their sake, he explains the gateways of deliverance;
though there are various dharmas, he teaches only the Single Vehicle Dharma,
which is the Great Vehicle.
At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
All non-Buddhists give rise to the false discrimination of impermanence."
The World-Honored One has also said that all conditioned phenomena are impermanent and subject to arising and ceasing.
What is the meaning of this?
Is it erroneous or correct?
"How many kinds of impermanence are there?
The Buddha told Mahāmati:
"All non-Buddhists maintain seven kinds of impermanence; these do not belong to my teaching."
What are the seven?
Some say that having performed [an action] and then abandoning it is called impermanence.
Others say that the destruction of form and location is called impermanence.
Some say that form itself is impermanent.
Others say that the interval during which form undergoes transformation is called impermanence;

the immediate disintegration of its own nature, like the transformation of milk into curd, is invisible in the interim, yet it is the destruction of impermanence through which all natures undergo change.
Some say that nature is impermanent;
some say that both nature and non-nature are impermanent;
and some say that the non-arising of all phenomena is impermanence, which enters into all phenomena.
Mahāmati! Regarding the impermanence of existence and non-existence: this refers to the destruction of the specific characteristics of the four great elements and their derivatives.
The self-nature of the four great elements is unobtainable; they are unborn.
That which is "non-arising impermanence" is neither permanence nor impermanence.

All phenomena, whether existent or non-existent, do not arise; even when analyzed down to the finest atom, they cannot be seen. This meaning of non-arising is not arising; this is called the characteristic of non-arising impermanence.
If one does not realize this, one falls into the view of all externalists that birth is impermanent in nature. Mahāmati!
That which is impermanent by nature is a false discrimination of one's own mind; it is not the nature of permanence or impermanence.
Why is this? Because the self-nature of impermanence is indestructible, Mahāmati!
This is the matter of the impermanence of all things, both existent and non-existent.
Apart from impermanence, there is nothing else capable of causing all dharmas to become non-existent,
just as a staff, a tile, or a stone destroys various objects.
It is directly perceived that each is not different; this nature is the phenomenon of impermanence, wherein there is no distinction between the agent and the acted-upon.
This is impermanence; this is the phenomenon.
If the agent and the action were non-different, then all natures would be eternal and devoid of causality.

Mahāmati, all natures are neither existent nor non-existent and possess causes; this is not something known by the ignorant and foolish, nor does it arise from causes that are dissimilar to the effect.
If things were produced, all natures would be entirely impermanent;
this would be an inconsistent state of affairs,
as there would be no distinction between the agent and the action.
Yet all are seen to be distinct.
If nature were impermanent, it would fall into the category of being a causal factor with a specific characteristic.
If it were to fall [into such a category], then no nature would be ultimate.
If all natures fall into the characteristic of being produced by causes, then that which is itself impermanent should be impermanent.
Since impermanence is impermanent, all natures would not be impermanent; they should therefore be permanent.
If impermanence were to enter into all natures, it would necessarily fall within the three periods of time.
That past form is accompanied by destruction; future form does not arise because form does not arise [in the future]; and present form is accompanied by the characteristic of destruction.
Form (*rūpa*) is a differentiation of the accumulation of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*).
The intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the four great elements and the derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*) is indestructible, because it is free from being either different or non-different [from them].

For all non-Buddhists, the four great elements are indestructible; however, for all that exists within the three realms of existence (*traidhātuka*), the four great elements and the derived matter exist as objects of knowledge (*jñeya*) subject to arising and ceasing.
Apart from the derived matter of the four great elements, upon what do all non-Buddhists contemplate impermanence?
The four great elements are unarisen, for their self-nature and characteristics are indestructible.
That which is devoid of initial creation and impermanence is not the four great elements (*mahābhūta*).
Furthermore, there exists something distinct from the four great elements, each possessing its own distinct characteristic.
Because it is their intrinsic nature (*svalakṣaṇa*), no differentiation can be apprehended; thus, they are without differentiation.
These things do not undergo further creation; because they are not produced through the two types of conditions, one should know that they are impermanent.
As for the impermanence of the destruction of form and location, it means that the four great elements and the derived matter do not perish, remaining ultimately indestructible.
Mahāmati! As for "ultimate," it means that when analyzed down to the smallest atom, one observes its destruction.
The four great elements and the derived forms and locations are seen as distinct; length and shortness cannot be apprehended, for they are not the four great elements.
The four great elements do not perish; it is their manifested form that appears to perish.
This falls into the Sāṃkhya school.
As for "form is impermanent," this means that form itself is impermanent.
That which has form and location is impermanent, yet it is not the four great elements (*mahābhūta*).
If the four great elements were impermanent, they would not be conventional designations (*saṃvṛti*).
If conventional designations lacked intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), one would fall into the worldly theory (*lokavāda*).
To see all natures as being merely verbal designations and not seeing the manifestation of their own-characteristic marks—
that which is called "transformational impermanence" refers to the appearance of the distinct natures of form, and not the four great elements themselves.
Just as when gold is fashioned into an ornament, it appears through transformation, yet the nature of the gold is not destroyed; rather, only the location of the ornament is destroyed.
So it is with the transformation of other natures and so forth.
Such are the various false conceptions of the non-eternalism held by the outsiders.
When the four great elements are burned by fire, their own specific characteristics are not burned.
If each of these specific characteristics were to perish, then the derived matter produced from the four great elements would necessarily be annihilated.
Mahāmati!
The arising of my Dharma is neither eternal nor non-eternal. Why is this so?

This means that because external objects are not fixed, it is taught that there is only the subtle mind of the three realms of existence; it does not teach that various characteristics have arising and ceasing.
Because the four great elements and their derivative forms are merely a combination of these elements, the two kinds of things—grasping and the grasped—are but products of false imagination.

Knowing these two kinds of false imagination (*vikalpa*), one leaves behind the two views of external existence and non-existence, awakening to the manifestation of what is measured by one's own mind.
False imagination arises from the activity of conceptualization; it is not that it does not engage in such activity.
Free from the delusive thoughts of existence and non-existence regarding the nature of the mind, all dharmas—whether mundane, supramundane, or supreme—are neither eternal nor impermanent.
Failing to realize that these are manifestations of one's own mind, one falls into the continuous succession of the evil views of the two extremes.

All non-Buddhists fail to realize that these are their own deluded imaginings; these ordinary people lack any fundamental basis for what they call the worldly, the world-transcending, and the supreme world-transcending dharmas, which arise from the discourse on deluded imagination and are not realized by the ignorant and foolish.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning,
spoke these verses: “Detached from initial creation, And distinct from the diversity of forms and locations,
The nature and form are impermanent— Such are the deluded false imaginings of the non-Buddhists.”
All natures are indestructible; they abide in their own great intrinsic nature.
Yet the non-Buddhists conceive of impermanence, submerged as they are in various views.
For those non-Buddhists, there is neither arising nor ceasing.
The nature of the Great Self is eternal; how can one speak of the perception of impermanence?
All things are merely the measure of the mind; the two kinds of mind revolve:
the grasper and the grasped, wherein there is neither self nor what belongs to a self.
"Brahmā is the root of the tree; its branches extend everywhere.
Thus have I taught: it is solely the measure of that mind.
At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
We pray that you will explain for us the sequential continuity of the meditative absorptions (*nirodha-samāpatti*) of all bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas.

If we and other bodhisattvas become skilled in the characteristics of this sequential continuity of the meditative absorptions of cessation, we shall never again recklessly abandon the gateway to the bliss of the meditative absorption of cessation, nor fall into the delusions of any śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, or non-Buddhists.”
The Buddha told Mahāmati:
"Listen attentively, listen attentively!
Reflect upon it well, and I shall explain it for you."
Mahāmati said to the Buddha:
“World-Honored One,
I pray that you will explain this for me.”
The Buddha told Mahāmati:
"Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas and śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas from the sixth stage onward enter the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*).

Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas of the seventh stage, however, enter meditative absorption in every thought-moment; they enter an absorption that is free from the characteristics of the self-nature of all phenomena (*sarva-dharma-svabhāva-lakṣaṇa*), which is not [the attainment] of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas."

All śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas fall into conditioned practice; they enter meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) that extinguish the marks of the grasper and the grasped. Therefore, in the seventh stage, there is no meditative attainment of mindfulness.

Having attained the non-differentiated mark of all dharmas, they do not partially attain the nature of various marks; they awaken to the meditative attainment of the nature and marks of the wholesome and unwholesome of all dharmas. Therefore, in the seventh stage, there is no meditative attainment of wholesome mindfulness.

Mahāmati! At the eighth stage, the Bodhisattvas, as well as the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, extinguish the conceptual characteristics of mind (*citta*), intellect (*manas*), and mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).

From the first stage up to the seventh stage, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas contemplate the extent of mind, intellect, and mental consciousness within the triple world; they abandon the notions of "I" and "mine," yet because they cultivate based on their own conceptualizations, they fall into the various external characteristics of objective phenomena.

"O Mahāmati, fools have two kinds of self-mind: the grasper and the grasped. Directed toward ignorance, they do not realize the faults and evils of beginningless time, being perfumed by the habitual tendencies of falsehood."
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas of the eighth stage, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas enter nirvāṇa.
However, because bodhisattvas are sustained by the awakening of samādhi, they do not enter parinirvāṇa despite the bliss of the gates of samādhi.

If one does not uphold it, the stage of a Tathāgata will remain unfulfilled, all activities for the sake of sentient beings will be abandoned, and the lineage of the Buddhas will be severed; therefore, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, manifest the inconceivable and immeasurable merits of a Tathāgata.
The śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, being led by their attachment to the attainment of pleasure within the gateways of samādhi, conceive the notion that this is nirvāṇa. Mahāmati!

I have established the divisions of the seven stages (*bhūmi*), in which one skillfully cultivates the characteristics of the mind, the intellect, and the mental consciousness; skillfully cultivates the notions of "self" and "what belongs to self"; masters the grasping of the selflessness of persons and phenomena; and thoroughly understands the characteristics of arising and ceasing, as well as the specific and general characteristics. Having attained mastery in the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) and the power of certainty through the gateways of samādhi, one proceeds through the successive stages of the path and enters the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*).

To prevent bodhisattva-mahāsattvas from failing to realize their own and shared characteristics, and from falling onto the deviant paths of externalists due to a lack of skill regarding the seven stages, the sequential order of the stages is established.
Mahāmati! In reality, there is neither arising nor ceasing, apart from what is manifested by one's own mind.
That which is called the sequential succession of the stages (*bhūmi*), as well as the various activities within the triple world, are not perceived by the foolish.

That which is not realized by the foolish refers to what I and the Buddhas have taught regarding the sequential succession of the stages (*bhūmi*), as well as the various activities within the three realms.
"Furthermore, Mahāmati!"

Śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and those on the eighth stage of the bodhisattva are intoxicated by the intoxication of the bliss of the cessation-samādhi; they do not understand that [the world] is a manifestation of their own minds, being obstructed by the habitual tendencies of their own and common characteristics.
Falling into the views of grasping at the selflessness of persons and the selflessness of dharmas, they falsely imagine nirvana; this is not the awakening of the wisdom of true cessation. Mahāmati!

A bodhisattva perceives the bliss of the gate of the samādhi of cessation, yet through their original vow, compassion, and the fulfillment of great pity, they understand the ten inexhaustible phrases and do not falsely imagine the notion of nirvana.
